management.safety: Do not give unlimited fluid boluses to a child with shock and depressed LV function; monitor for pulmonary oedema.
management.local: Perth Children's Hospital Clinical Care of Paediatric Patients with COVID-19, PIMS-TS guidance and local multidisciplinary protocol.

skill: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus / nasociliary involvement
stem: A 63-year-old presents with two days of painful unilateral forehead vesicles and a rash extending to the tip of the nose. The right eye is watery and photophobic, but visual acuity is only mildly reduced. She is immunocompetent and has no prior history of eye disease. A colleague suggests topical antibiotic ointment alone.
ask: What is the safest management priority?
options: Treat with topical antibiotics alone because nasal vesicles are not linked to ocular disease.
Delay treatment until vesicles crust because antiviral therapy is ineffective before healing begins.
Arrange routine optometry review after one week if visual acuity continues to deteriorate.
Start prompt systemic antiviral therapy and arrange urgent ophthalmological assessment.
Give topical corticosteroids immediately without slit-lamp review to prevent ocular scarring.
explanations: Topical antibiotics do not treat varicella-zoster virus or prevent keratitis and uveitis. Nasal-tip involvement raises concern for nasociliary nerve involvement.
Systemic antivirals are most useful when initiated early and can still be appropriate later with ocular disease. Waiting for crusting misses a therapeutic opportunity.
Photophobia and eye watering with a V1 rash indicate possible ocular inflammation requiring prompt evaluation; visual acuity can be preserved early.

Correct: suspect herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign, initiate systemic antivirals promptly and contact ophthalmology urgently for slit-lamp examination and follow-up. Evaluate immunosuppression and complications.
Topical steroids can worsen some corneal infections and should be directed by an ophthalmologist after assessing ocular involvement. They are not a substitute for antiviral therapy.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip of the nose signal nasociliary involvement and increase the risk of herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
pivot: A localised thoracic shingles eruption without ocular or neurological involvement usually follows a less urgent outpatient antiviral pathway.

steps: Assess
Document V1 distribution, Hutchinson sign, vision, photophobia and ocular redness.
Treat
Start appropriate systemic antiviral treatment promptly after renal function and contraindication review.
Refer
Contact ophthalmology urgently for corneal, anterior chamber and intraocular assessment.
Follow
Provide pain management, infection-control advice and clear return precautions for visual changes.
management.safety: Do not prescribe unsupervised topical ocular steroids for suspected herpetic eye disease.
management.local: Victorian Department of Health Protocol for Management of Herpes Zoster, February 2026.

skill: Classic galactosaemia / jaundice and E. coli sepsis after milk feeds
stem: A 10-day-old term infant develops poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice and lethargy after initially appearing well. Examination shows hepatomegaly and cataracts; blood cultures later grow E. coli. Liver enzymes are elevated and coagulation is prolonged. The infant has been exclusively breastfed and the newborn screening result is pending.
ask: Which disease-specific action is most appropriate alongside sepsis treatment?
options: Continue breastfeeding because breast milk is protective against all neonatal metabolic disorders.
Switch to a lactose-containing formula to maintain calorie intake during intravenous antibiotic treatment.
Wait for newborn screening confirmation before altering feeds because false-positive results are common.
Treat with phototherapy alone because jaundice is the major clinical manifestation of the illness.
Stop galactose exposure immediately and initiate lactose-free feeding with metabolic specialist input.
explanations: Breast milk contains lactose, which yields galactose and can worsen organ toxicity in classic galactosaemia. Feeding advice differs from most neonatal illnesses.
Standard cow-milk formulas contain lactose and can perpetuate galactose accumulation. A specialist-recommended lactose-free formula is needed.
The constellation of liver dysfunction, cataracts and E. coli sepsis strongly suggests classic galactosaemia; delaying dietary treatment while awaiting screening risks harm.
Phototherapy may be needed for elevated unconjugated bilirubin but does not address the enzyme defect, liver injury or infection. Sepsis and metabolic treatment are both urgent.

Correct: suspect GALT deficiency, stop breast milk and lactose-containing formula immediately, start a suitable galactose-free formula, confirm enzymatic/metabolite testing and treat E. coli sepsis and organ dysfunction.
pearl: A newborn with jaundice, liver failure, cataracts and E. coli sepsis after milk feeding should prompt urgent suspicion of classic galactosaemia.
pivot: A thriving jaundiced neonate with normal feeding, normal direct bilirubin and no systemic illness is more likely to have physiological jaundice.

steps: Stabilise
Admit for neonatal sepsis care, support circulation and check glucose, coagulation and liver function.
Remove trigger
Stop breast milk and lactose-containing formula and initiate appropriate lactose/galactose-free nutrition.
Confirm
Send newborn screen follow-up, RBC GALT activity and galactose-1-phosphate testing with metabolic advice.
Continue care
Treat proven infection, monitor organ function and arrange long-term metabolic and developmental follow-up.
management.safety: Do not wait for the newborn screening result before restricting galactose when classic disease is strongly suspected.
management.local: WA Newborn Bloodspot Screening Program: Galactosaemia, clinical features and lactose-free treatment.

skill: MASLD / high-risk fibrosis score despite mild transaminitis
stem: A 52-year-old with type 2 diabetes and central adiposity has ultrasound-confirmed hepatic steatosis. ALT is 58 U/L, AST 66 U/L and platelets 145 × 10⁹/L. Viral hepatitis and substantial alcohol exposure have been excluded. His calculated FIB-4 score is 3.1. He feels well and has no ascites or jaundice.
ask: Which next action most appropriately addresses his liver-related risk?
options: Arrange fibrosis assessment and specialist referral while managing cardiometabolic risks in primary care.
Repeat the liver ultrasound annually because mild transaminitis excludes clinically important advanced fibrosis.
Start empirical corticosteroids because a high FIB-4 score is diagnostic of autoimmune hepatitis.
Reassure that normal bilirubin rules out cirrhosis and stop further liver investigations.
Prescribe a liver detoxification supplement and defer referral until portal hypertension appears.
explanations: Correct: FIB-4 above approximately 2.67 in an at-risk adult suggests possible advanced fibrosis, requiring further assessment with elastography and/or hepatology referral. Evaluate other causes and address diabetes, alcohol, lipids and cardiovascular risk.
Ultrasound detects fat but cannot reliably stage fibrosis. Mild aminotransferase elevation is compatible with advanced disease; annual imaging alone misses risk stratification and timely treatment.

FIB-4 is a noninvasive fibrosis risk tool, not an autoimmune hepatitis diagnostic test. Steroids could worsen diabetes and cause harm without autoimmune serology, immunoglobulins and specialist assessment.
Normal bilirubin and preserved synthetic function do not exclude significant fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis. The high score is the decisive clue despite few symptoms.
Unregulated supplements have no established role in treating advanced fibrosis and may cause hepatotoxicity. Waiting for decompensation forfeits an opportunity for preventive care.
pearl: In adults with metabolic fatty liver, FIB-4 >2.67 is a referral-level fibrosis signal even when ALT and bilirubin seem reassuring.
pivot: A low FIB-4 in an appropriate age group can support primary-care metabolic management with planned reassessment, rather than immediate specialist staging.

steps: Verify risk
Review alcohol, medicines, viral serology, platelet trends and other chronic liver disease causes.
Stage fibrosis
Arrange transient elastography or another validated second-line fibrosis test and hepatology assessment.
Reduce risk
Optimise diabetes, blood pressure, lipids, physical activity and nutrition using shared decisions.
Follow through
Assess cirrhosis-related surveillance needs if advanced fibrosis is confirmed and arrange coordinated follow-up.
management.safety: FIB-4 performance is age dependent; do not use the same threshold uncritically in patients younger than 35 or older than 65.
management.local: RACGP-endorsed Australian MAFLD primary-care consensus statement, FIB-4 referral thresholds.

skill: Septic miscarriage / antibiotics and uterine source control
stem: A 28-year-old at approximately 10 weeks' gestation presents with two days of heavy bleeding, fever and lower abdominal pain. She is tachycardic at 126/min, BP 93/57 mmHg, with uterine tenderness and offensive vaginal discharge. Ultrasound shows heterogeneous material within the uterine cavity and no viable pregnancy. Lactate is 3.1 mmol/L.
ask: What is the best coordinated initial management?
options: Give oral antibiotics and arrange an elective ultrasound in one week after the bleeding settles.
Resuscitate, start broad IV antibiotics and arrange urgent gynaecological evacuation after stabilisation.
Administer misoprostol alone and discharge because ultrasound confirms that the pregnancy is nonviable.
Delay antibiotics until endometrial cultures return so the treatment can be precisely targeted.
Provide anti-D alone and monitor for spontaneous passage of products without surgical review.
explanations: Oral outpatient treatment cannot safely address haemodynamic compromise, sepsis and retained infected tissue. A week of delay risks septic shock and disseminated infection.

Correct: activate sepsis care, take appropriate cultures without delaying IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, restore perfusion and involve senior gynaecology urgently for uterine source control. Evaluate anti-D need separately.

Misoprostol can be appropriate for selected stable noninfected pregnancy loss, but shock physiology and suspected uterine infection require inpatient resuscitation and definitive source-control planning.
Waiting for cultures postpones life-saving empiric treatment. Samples may be collected promptly, with therapy subsequently refined using results and clinical response.
Anti-D may be relevant for an RhD-negative patient under local protocols, but it does not treat infection or remove retained infected products. Observation alone is unsafe here.
pearl: Fever, uterine tenderness, malodorous discharge and retained products after pregnancy loss indicate a septic miscarriage until proven otherwise.
pivot: An afebrile haemodynamically stable patient with early pregnancy loss may choose expectant, medical or surgical management after counselling.

steps: Resuscitate
Assess ABCDE, monitor haemodynamics, give IV fluids as indicated and obtain urgent senior/anaesthetic help.
Treat sepsis
Send blood and relevant genital tract cultures promptly and give local-protocol broad IV antimicrobial cover.
Control source
Arrange urgent gynaecology assessment and evacuation of infected retained products once appropriately stabilised.
Review
Monitor lactate, urine output, bleeding and organ function; provide RhD and reproductive follow-up where indicated.
management.safety: Do not delay antibiotics or source-control consultation for a repeat scan, culture results or an outpatient misoprostol trial.
management.local: RANZCOG Miscarriage, Recurrent Miscarriage and Ectopic Pregnancy Clinical Guideline (2025), alongside the Australian sepsis standard.

skill: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis / valve intervention referral
stem: A 78-year-old with a harsh ejection systolic murmur has developed exertional chest tightness and two episodes of near-syncope. Echocardiography shows a heavily calcified aortic valve, peak velocity 4.4 m/s, mean gradient 48 mmHg and left ventricular ejection fraction 57%. She is currently pain-free and normotensive.
ask: Which management decision most improves her prognosis?
options: Arrange annual echocardiography only because preserved ejection fraction indicates a compensated valve lesion.
Commence a long-acting nitrate as definitive therapy for the fixed outflow obstruction.
Refer promptly to a multidisciplinary valve team for definitive aortic valve replacement assessment.
Advise unrestricted exercise because symptoms occur only during physical exertion and not at rest.
Start high-dose diuretics empirically and defer specialist assessment until heart failure develops.
explanations: Observation may be appropriate for selected asymptomatic disease, but exertional angina and presyncope with severe gradients mark symptomatic high-risk aortic stenosis requiring definitive assessment.
Nitrates can reduce preload and worsen hypotension in significant fixed outflow obstruction; they do not correct the narrowed valve or improve long-term survival.

Correct: symptomatic severe aortic stenosis warrants prompt cardiology and heart-team evaluation for transcatheter or surgical aortic valve replacement, incorporating anatomy, frailty, preferences and procedural risk.
Exertional presyncope and angina are warning symptoms, not reassurance. Strenuous activity before evaluation may provoke haemodynamic collapse.
Diuretics may relieve selected congestion but excessive preload reduction can worsen output, and medication does not replace valve intervention in symptomatic severe stenosis.
pearl: Symptoms plus severe aortic stenosis mean urgent valve-team assessment even when the ejection fraction is normal.
pivot: A truly asymptomatic patient with moderate stenosis and preserved ventricular function may be followed with scheduled echocardiography.

steps: Assess severity
Confirm symptom chronology, echocardiographic gradients, valve area and ventricular function.
Escalate
Arrange prompt specialist cardiology and multidisciplinary valve assessment for SAVR versus TAVI.
Reduce harm
Review exertional safety and avoid indiscriminate preload-reducing medication or hypotension.
Plan care
Evaluate coronary disease, comorbidities, procedural risk and patient goals before intervention.
management.safety: Preserved ejection fraction does not make symptomatic severe aortic stenosis safe for watchful waiting.
management.local: CSANZ Australian ARF/RHD Guideline 2025, aortic stenosis section: severe symptomatic disease merits AVR assessment.

skill: Heavy menstrual bleeding from menarche / screen for bleeding disorder
stem: A 15-year-old reports flooding through pads since her first period, with bleeding lasting eight to ten days. She also has frequent epistaxis and bruises easily; her mother needed treatment for bleeding after dental extraction. Hb is 93 g/L, ferritin is low and pregnancy testing is negative. She is haemodynamically stable.
ask: What is the most appropriate next management approach?
options: Arrange pelvic ultrasound first because structural uterine lesions explain most adolescent heavy periods.
Reassure that anovulatory cycles explain the symptoms and exclude a haemostatic disorder.
Start anticoagulation to prevent menstrual blood clotting while awaiting a haematology appointment.
Treat bleeding and iron deficiency while arranging targeted assessment for von Willebrand disease.
Schedule endometrial biopsy as the initial investigation because the menstrual bleeding began at menarche.
explanations: Structural causes are relatively uncommon in adolescents, and ultrasound is not routinely first-line without atypical findings. The mucocutaneous and family history point toward a haemostatic problem.
Anovulatory bleeding is common after menarche, but lifelong heavy flow with epistaxis, bruising and familial bleeding merits evaluation for an inherited disorder.
Anticoagulation can aggravate uterine bleeding and has no indication here. Acute management aims to stabilise haemostasis and correct iron depletion.

Correct: assess severity and consent, give appropriate hormonal or tranexamic therapy and iron, and arrange coagulation and von Willebrand evaluation with haematology. Timing of specialised assays matters during acute bleeding.
Endometrial malignancy is exceptionally uncommon in this setting. Invasive sampling does not address the strong bleeding-disorder history and is not the first investigation.
pearl: Heavy periods from menarche plus epistaxis or family bleeding history should trigger a von Willebrand disease assessment.
pivot: Isolated mild heavy flow without anaemia or a bleeding history may be managed with symptom-focused care and reassessment.

steps: Assess
Review haemodynamic stability, bleeding quantity, pregnancy possibility and confidentiality.
Treat
Provide iron replacement and suitable tranexamic or hormonal bleeding control with contraindication checks.
Investigate
Check FBC/ferritin and targeted haemostatic tests; plan von Willebrand studies outside confounding acute circumstances.
Coordinate
Refer to adolescent gynaecology/haematology and establish a menstrual symptom and haemoglobin follow-up plan.
management.safety: A normal routine PT or APTT does not exclude von Willebrand disease; specialised testing needs correct timing and interpretation.
management.local: Royal Children's Hospital adolescent heavy menstrual bleeding clinical practice guideline.

skill: Measles exposure in immunocompromised child / post-exposure immunoglobulin
stem: A 9-year-old undergoing chemotherapy for leukaemia spent several hours in the same room as a child subsequently confirmed to have measles. Exposure was four days ago. Measles IgG is negative and the child has no fever or rash. The parents ask whether an MMR vaccine today would provide adequate protection.
ask: What is the most appropriate preventive response?
options: Give MMR immediately because the live vaccine works even during intensive chemotherapy.
Wait for fever or rash before contacting public health because prophylaxis is ineffective after 72 hours.
Offer oral antiviral medication as routine measles prophylaxis and avoid further contact tracing.
Repeat measles IgG in three weeks before deciding whether post-exposure prophylaxis is warranted.
Arrange normal human immunoglobulin urgently with public-health and oncology specialist advice.
explanations: MMR is a live vaccine and is generally contraindicated in severe chemotherapy-associated immunosuppression. It is not a substitute for indicated passive prophylaxis in this child.
The child is susceptible and within the six-day window for immunoglobulin. Waiting for symptoms sacrifices the opportunity to reduce disease severity and spread.
No routinely recommended oral antiviral prevents measles after exposure. Contact management instead uses immunity assessment, immunoglobulin or vaccination according to risk.
Repeat serology weeks later cannot protect during the current exposure window. Negative IgG now and severe immunosuppression warrant immediate action.
Correct: notify the public-health unit and oncology team, administer recommended normal human immunoglobulin within six days of exposure, and provide exposure and symptom monitoring advice.
pearl: Susceptible immunocompromised measles contacts need urgent NHIG within six days; live MMR is not an appropriate substitute.
pivot: An immunocompetent susceptible person seen within 72 hours may instead qualify for post-exposure MMR under Australian guidance.

steps: Notify
Contact the local public-health unit and treating oncology team immediately.
Protect
Arrange indicated NHIG according to age, weight, immunocompromise and exposure timing.
Limit spread
Follow public-health exclusion and infection-control instructions; advise calling ahead if symptoms develop.
Follow up
Document immune status and prophylaxis, monitor symptoms and revisit future immunisation when safe.
management.safety: Do not administer a live MMR vaccine to a severely immunocompromised chemotherapy patient without specialist immunisation clearance.
management.local: Australian Immunisation Handbook: measles post-exposure prophylaxis table, six-day NHIG window.

skill: Recent carotid TIA / time-sensitive endarterectomy for severe stenosis
stem: A 69-year-old had 20 minutes of right arm weakness and expressive dysphasia two days ago. Symptoms resolved, and brain MRI shows no acute infarct. Carotid imaging demonstrates 82% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery by NASCET criteria, with no contralateral significant disease. He is neurologically intact and medically fit for surgery.
ask: What is the most appropriate stroke-prevention strategy now?
options: Arrange urgent vascular assessment for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within two weeks of symptoms.
Schedule routine surveillance imaging because a resolved deficit means the carotid lesion is asymptomatic.
Choose carotid stenting automatically because it carries lower perioperative stroke risk than surgery.
Defer any carotid intervention until three months have passed to minimise the risk of recurrence.
Treat only with anticoagulation because symptomatic carotid plaques respond best to direct oral anticoagulants.
explanations: Correct: severe ipsilateral symptomatic stenosis after a nondisabling carotid-territory TIA has a strong evidence-based indication for timely carotid endarterectomy by an experienced low-complication team, alongside intensive medical prevention.
Symptom resolution does not make the lesion asymptomatic. Early recurrent stroke risk is greatest soon after a TIA, so routine interval surveillance misses a window of benefit.
Stenting may be reasonable in selected anatomical or procedural circumstances, but endarterectomy is generally preferred because of lower periprocedural stroke risk in many patients.
Delaying surgery beyond the early symptomatic period reduces the opportunity to prevent recurrent events. Operative timing should be coordinated urgently after specialist assessment.
Anticoagulation is indicated for specific cardioembolic causes such as atrial fibrillation, not as a routine substitute for treating symptomatic high-grade atherosclerotic carotid stenosis.
pearl: Symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis after a nondisabling TIA is an early endarterectomy indication, ideally within 14 days.
pivot: A patient with complete carotid occlusion or a disabling large infarct needs a different specialist risk-benefit discussion, not automatic early endarterectomy.

steps: Identify territory
Confirm the TIA symptoms match the ipsilateral carotid lesion and exclude haemorrhage or major infarction.
Refer urgently
Contact the stroke and vascular teams for early endarterectomy assessment by an audited specialist service.
Prevent recurrence
Start or optimise antiplatelet, lipid-lowering and vascular risk-factor therapy according to stroke guidance.
Plan procedure
Review cardiac fitness, anatomy, patient preferences and perioperative stroke/bleeding risk.
management.safety: Do not equate resolved symptoms with a low-risk asymptomatic stenosis; early recurrent stroke remains possible.
management.local: Stroke Foundation Australian 2025 emergency clinical guideline summary: carotid surgery, 70–99% stenosis and ideally within two weeks.

skill: First-episode psychosis / exclude reversible causes and initiate coordinated care
stem: A 19-year-old university student has withdrawn socially and developed persecutory beliefs and auditory hallucinations over six weeks. He sleeps poorly and occasionally uses cannabis. He is frightened but cooperative, denies immediate self-harm intent and has no fever, focal neurological signs or fluctuating consciousness. His family requests antipsychotics without any medical assessment.
ask: Which initial approach best balances diagnostic safety and timely treatment?
options: Diagnose schizophrenia immediately because six weeks of hallucinations excludes other causes of psychosis.
Arrange comprehensive risk and medical/substance assessment with early psychosis referral and shared treatment planning.
Provide only cannabis abstinence advice and defer psychiatric assessment until all symptoms have resolved.
Start high-dose antipsychotic medication without baseline physical observations or a medication-risk discussion.
Order extensive autoimmune panels for every patient and withhold any supportive care until results return.
explanations: Schizophrenia requires a longer overall disturbance and exclusion of substance or medical causes; six weeks of psychosis is not enough to assume the final diagnosis.

Correct: assess safety, substances, physical and neurological red flags, basic medical causes and functioning; engage an early psychosis service, offer family-inclusive care with consent and consider appropriate antipsychotic treatment with baseline metabolic monitoring.
Cannabis may contribute to symptoms but does not justify abandoning assessment or treatment. Persistent psychosis requires clinical review and coordinated support even when substance use is present.
Antipsychotics can help, but avoid unnecessary high initial doses and check weight, BP, metabolic risk, adverse-effect vulnerability and informed preferences before a treatment plan.

Autoimmune encephalitis investigations are indicated when red flags such as seizures, dyskinesia, autonomic instability or altered consciousness arise; indiscriminate panels can delay care and mislead.
pearl: First-episode psychosis is a syndrome requiring safety, medical and substance assessment; do not label schizophrenia prematurely.
pivot: Rapid fluctuating confusion, fever, seizures or new neurological deficits would shift priority toward urgent delirium or encephalitis evaluation.

steps: Assess safety
Evaluate suicidality, aggression risk, command hallucinations, capacity, self-care and available supports.
Screen causes
Take medication/substance history, examine physical and neurological status, and order targeted initial tests.
Engage services
Refer promptly to early intervention psychiatry and collaboratively discuss psychosocial and pharmacological options.
Monitor
Record baseline weight/BMI, BP and relevant metabolic parameters before ongoing antipsychotic treatment.
management.safety: Avoid both premature schizophrenia labelling and delaying care for indiscriminate testing; red flags mandate urgent medical escalation.
management.local: Orygen Australian Medical Management in Early Psychosis manual: comprehensive assessment, treatment and physical-health monitoring.

skill: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding / urgent haemostatic correction
stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed infant develops increasing sleepiness, vomiting and a new bulging fontanelle. The parents declined neonatal vitamin K prophylaxis. Examination shows scattered bruises; head imaging reveals intracranial haemorrhage. PT/INR is markedly prolonged, platelets and fibrinogen are normal and there is no family bleeding history.
ask: Which immediate targeted treatment is most appropriate alongside neurocritical resuscitation?
options: Begin oral iron supplementation because breastfed infants commonly develop iron-related bleeding.
Administer prophylactic intramuscular vitamin K only and discharge once the fontanelle softens.
Give urgent parenteral vitamin K with specialist-guided coagulation factor replacement as required.
Wait for a full inherited bleeding-disorder panel before reversing the prolonged clotting time.
Treat with platelet transfusion alone because neonatal bruising indicates platelet failure.
explanations: Iron deficiency does not explain the extreme PT prolongation or intracranial haemorrhage. Nutritional supplementation cannot treat this life-threatening coagulation failure.

A routine prophylactic dose is insufficient as a stand-alone response to established intracranial bleeding; treatment needs monitored hospital-level haemostatic correction and neurosurgical assessment.

Correct: suspect late vitamin K deficiency bleeding, give urgent IV/parenteral phytomenadione under neonatal guidance and provide rapid factor replacement with FFP or other specialist-directed products when bleeding is critical.
Investigating alternative coagulopathies is appropriate, but waiting for a full panel delays potentially lifesaving vitamin K and haemostatic treatment in a strongly suggestive presentation.
Platelet count is normal, so isolated platelet transfusion does not correct vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency. Coagulation tests and imaging require urgent serial reassessment.
pearl: An unprotected breastfed infant with bleeding at 2–12 weeks and very prolonged PT/INR may have late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
pivot: Persistent abnormal coagulation after appropriate vitamin K replacement should prompt investigation of liver disease or an inherited coagulation disorder.

steps: Stabilise
Activate neonatal intensive care, assess airway and perfusion, and involve neurosurgery for intracranial bleeding.
Correct
Give specialist-guided parenteral vitamin K and rapid haemostatic factor replacement when severe bleeding requires it.
Investigate
Repeat PT/INR, APTT, fibrinogen, platelets and liver tests while assessing intracranial injury.
Prevent recurrence
Document prophylaxis history, counsel caregivers and investigate malabsorption or cholestasis if indicated.
management.safety: Life-threatening bleeding needs immediate haemostatic support; oral prophylaxis alone is not adequate treatment.
management.local: RCPA Manual: haemorrhagic disease of the newborn; NHMRC vitamin K prophylaxis recommendation.

skill: Maternal parvovirus B19 / fetal anaemia surveillance
stem: A 27-year-old childcare worker at 18 weeks' gestation develops mild arthralgia and a rash after a workplace parvovirus B19 outbreak. Maternal serology confirms recent infection. Ultrasound shows a normally grown fetus with no hydrops, and she feels well. She asks whether a single reassuring scan excludes any fetal complication.
ask: What is the most appropriate next antenatal plan?
options: Reassure that absence of hydrops today rules out later fetal anaemia and needs no further surveillance.
Recommend immediate delivery because parvovirus infection at 18 weeks always leads to fetal deterioration.
Give routine maternal antiviral treatment and repeat ultrasound only if maternal fever returns.
Refer for serial specialist ultrasound surveillance, including fetal anaemia assessment using MCA Doppler.
Offer maternal MMR vaccination because it provides cross-protection against fetal parvovirus infection.
explanations: Fetal anaemia or hydrops can develop after maternal infection even when the initial scan is normal. A single normal ultrasound cannot end surveillance.
Most maternal parvovirus infections do not cause serious fetal complications. At 18 weeks, delivery would cause extreme prematurity and is not indicated without severe fetal disease.
There is no established routine maternal antiviral treatment that prevents fetal anaemia from parvovirus B19. Management focuses on fetal monitoring and specialist intervention when needed.
Correct: refer to maternal fetal medicine for serial ultrasound and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity Doppler to detect evolving anaemia or hydrops over the subsequent weeks.
MMR targets measles, mumps and rubella, not parvovirus B19, and is contraindicated during pregnancy as a live vaccine.
pearl: Maternal parvovirus B19 can suppress fetal erythropoiesis; fetal anaemia may appear weeks after a reassuring initial scan.
pivot: Maternal IgG positive with IgM negative and no recent exposure evidence usually indicates past immunity rather than an acute fetal-risk episode.

steps: Confirm
Review maternal exposure history and interpret IgM/IgG with obstetric infectious-disease advice.
Refer
Arrange maternal fetal medicine review and serial ultrasound with MCA Doppler and hydrops assessment.
Escalate findings
Discuss suspected fetal anaemia with a fetal therapy centre for confirmatory assessment and possible transfusion.
Counsel
Explain that most pregnancies do well, provide warning advice and document follow-up intervals.
management.safety: Do not terminate surveillance after one normal scan; hydrops and fetal anaemia may be delayed.
management.local: Queensland Metro South GP Maternity Shared Care Education 2024, parvovirus B19 pregnancy risks and surveillance.

skill: Mild asthma / avoid SABA-only treatment
stem: A 23-year-old with confirmed asthma uses salbutamol for wheeze twice weekly. He has no night waking and normal spirometry between symptoms, but had an ED-treated exacerbation last year. He asks for another salbutamol prescription and declines daily inhaled treatment because he feels well most days.
ask: Which treatment discussion best follows current Australian asthma recommendations?
options: Continue salbutamol alone because intermittent symptoms make inhaled anti-inflammatory treatment unnecessary.
Replace salbutamol with a long-acting beta agonist alone to improve exercise tolerance safely.
Prescribe oral prednisolone whenever he exercises because it prevents all future exacerbations.
Use antibiotics as the regular reliever because most mild asthma exacerbations are infection-related.
Offer an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen, such as as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol.
explanations: SABA-only treatment increases severe exacerbation risk even in people with infrequent symptoms. His previous ED visit reinforces the need for anti-inflammatory treatment.
LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma and increases severe exacerbation risk; it must be paired with inhaled corticosteroid in an appropriate regimen.
Systemic corticosteroids have significant cumulative harms and are not a preventive substitute for regular or symptom-driven inhaled corticosteroid treatment.
Antibiotics do not treat underlying airway inflammation and are not routine reliever therapy. They are reserved for specific bacterial infections when clinically indicated.

Correct: explain exacerbation prevention and offer guideline-supported ICS-containing therapy, commonly low-dose budesonide–formoterol as needed, with inhaler technique training and a written action plan.
pearl: Adults and adolescents with asthma should not be managed with SABA alone, even when symptoms are infrequent.
pivot: More frequent symptoms or exacerbations may warrant maintenance-and-reliever therapy or step-up treatment after assessing adherence and technique.

steps: Assess control
Review symptoms, exacerbations, reliever use, triggers and risk factors for severe attacks.
Prescribe prevention
Discuss ICS-containing options and agree on a suitable regimen instead of SABA monotherapy.
Teach
Demonstrate inhaler technique and create a personalised written asthma action plan.
Review
Arrange follow-up to assess response, adherence, side effects and need for treatment adjustment.
management.safety: Never prescribe a long-acting beta agonist as monotherapy for asthma; ICS is required.
management.local: Australian Asthma Handbook, treatment levels for adults and adolescents, ICS–formoterol recommendation.

skill: Hepatitis C antibody positive / RNA negative interpretation
stem: A 46-year-old presents for routine screening. Hepatitis C antibody is positive but confirmatory HCV RNA is undetectable. He recalls a treated infection eight years ago, has normal liver enzymes and reports no new injecting or other blood exposure. He asks whether the positive antibody means he currently has transmissible hepatitis C.
ask: Which explanation and follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Explain that antibody may persist after clearance; assess reinfection risk and retest RNA if indicated.
Diagnose active chronic hepatitis C because any positive antibody confirms ongoing viraemia.
Start a direct-acting antiviral immediately despite undetectable HCV RNA and no recent exposure.
Repeat antibody titres monthly until they become negative to document a complete virological cure.
Advise that past infection confers lifelong immunity and no further testing is ever necessary.
explanations: Correct: anti-HCV reflects exposure and often remains positive after spontaneous or treatment-related clearance. An undetectable RNA usually means no current viraemia; review timing, ongoing risk and liver disease before deciding on repeat RNA testing.
Antibody positivity alone cannot distinguish resolved from active infection. Detectable RNA establishes current infection and guides antiviral treatment.
Direct-acting antivirals treat active HCV infection, not an antibody result without viraemia. Prescribing them now adds cost and potential harms without an indicated target.
Antibody titres are not used to monitor cure and may remain detectable indefinitely. Sustained virological response and reinfection assessment rely on RNA testing.
Prior HCV infection does not produce reliable protective immunity. Reinfection is possible, so prevention advice and RNA retesting remain relevant with new exposures.
pearl: HCV antibody positive with RNA negative usually means past cleared infection, not current viraemia; antibodies can persist for life.
pivot: A new recent high-risk exposure, unexplained elevated ALT or ongoing risk warrants repeat RNA despite an initially negative result.

steps: Interpret
Review antibody, confirmatory RNA, prior treatment and possible timing of new exposure.
Assess liver health
Evaluate other liver disease causes and fibrosis risk when relevant, especially after prior chronic infection.
Counsel
Explain antibody persistence, lack of reliable reinfection immunity and bloodborne virus prevention.
Retest selectively
Arrange HCV RNA follow-up if recent exposure, abnormal liver tests or ongoing reinfection risk emerges.
management.safety: Do not label a person currently infectious or prescribe antiviral therapy on antibody positivity alone.
management.local: ASHM National Hepatitis C Testing Policy 2025: conveying antibody-positive, RNA-negative results.

skill: ADHD stimulant assessment / exertional syncope as cardiac red flag
stem: A 12-year-old with a well-supported ADHD diagnosis has persistent school impairment despite behavioural strategies. His parents request methylphenidate. During baseline review, he describes fainting twice while sprinting at football training, and his uncle died suddenly aged 32. BP and resting heart rate are normal; no murmur is heard.
ask: What should happen before stimulant medication is initiated?
options: Begin methylphenidate immediately because normal resting observations exclude important inherited heart disease.
Seek specialist cardiac evaluation of exertional syncope and family history before medication initiation.
Order a routine ECG only and prescribe stimulants if the tracing has no obvious abnormality.
Avoid all ADHD treatment permanently because any family sudden death contraindicates psychological support.
Prescribe a sedating antipsychotic instead because it has no relevant cardiovascular adverse effects.
explanations: Normal resting BP, pulse and auscultation cannot exclude arrhythmogenic or structural disease. Exertional syncope and young sudden death in the family require targeted investigation.

Correct: refer for cardiology assessment and investigate possible inherited or exertional cardiac disease before starting a medicine that may increase heart rate and blood pressure. Continue nonpharmacological support.
An ECG is useful but a normal tracing does not exclude all causes of exertional syncope. A specialist assessment may require echocardiography, exercise testing or other studies.
A cardiac red flag delays prescribing pending assessment, not the entire ADHD care pathway. Educational and psychological supports should continue.
Antipsychotics are not an appropriate first-line substitute for ADHD and may themselves cause QT, metabolic or other adverse effects.
pearl: Exertional syncope and a young relative's sudden death are indications for cardiac review before ADHD stimulant therapy.
pivot: Without cardiac red flags, routine ECG is not universally required before starting stimulants; baseline pulse, BP and clinical history remain important.

steps: Characterise
Clarify exertional fainting, palpitations, family cardiac history and neurological mimics.
Refer
Arrange timely paediatric cardiology assessment and investigations directed by the specialist.
Support ADHD
Continue school accommodations and behavioural strategies while medication decisions are deferred.
Review plan
Revisit pharmacotherapy after cardiac risk assessment and monitor BP, pulse, growth and symptoms if prescribed.
management.safety: Do not use a normal resting ECG as a stand-alone clearance for exertional syncope with a concerning family history.
management.local: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD, pre-medication cardiovascular risk assessment.

skill: Crystal-proven gout flare / CKD and anticoagulant constraints
stem: A 73-year-old with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m²) and atrial fibrillation on apixaban presents with a painful swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial aspirate shows monosodium urate crystals, Gram stain is negative and there are no systemic infection features. He requests his usual high-dose ibuprofen and colchicine.
ask: Which acute anti-inflammatory strategy is safest to consider?
options: Use full-dose ibuprofen because a single short course does not affect kidney function or bleeding.
Give repeated high-dose colchicine until diarrhoea develops because the renal clearance is unchanged.
Consider corticosteroid treatment after excluding joint infection, avoiding high-risk NSAID and colchicine dosing.
Increase apixaban temporarily because joint inflammation increases the risk of local thrombosis and embolism.
Withhold all analgesia until serum urate falls spontaneously, then begin urate-lowering medication.
explanations: NSAIDs can worsen renal function and increase bleeding when combined with anticoagulation. Severe CKD makes routine full-dose ibuprofen an unsafe first choice.
Colchicine accumulates in significant renal impairment and can cause severe toxicity, especially with interacting medicines. Repeated high doses are not justified.

Correct: after reasonable exclusion of septic arthritis, a short systemic or intra-articular corticosteroid regimen may control a crystal-proven flare while avoiding NSAID renal/bleeding risks and excessive colchicine exposure.
Apixaban treats thromboembolic risk from atrial fibrillation; increasing its dose does not reduce urate crystal inflammation and may cause bleeding.
Acute pain and inflammation should be treated promptly. Serum urate can be misleading during a flare, and urate-lowering plans are separate from immediate symptom control.
pearl: Acute gout treatment must account for kidney function, anticoagulants and drug interactions; corticosteroids can be useful when NSAIDs and colchicine are risky.
pivot: A febrile hot joint or suspicious synovial findings requires urgent septic arthritis assessment despite the presence of urate crystals.

steps: Exclude infection
Review fever, systemic signs, joint aspirate culture and risk factors for septic arthritis.
Choose therapy
Use a suitable corticosteroid approach with renal, diabetes and infection risks considered.
Avoid harm
Avoid routine NSAIDs and excessive colchicine in advanced CKD and with anticoagulant exposure.
Prevent recurrence
Review urate-lowering therapy, interacting drugs and future flare prophylaxis with renal-safe planning.
management.safety: Urate crystals do not absolutely exclude concurrent septic arthritis; reassess if symptoms or cultures suggest infection.
management.local: RACGP gout management review: acute flare options and colchicine dose caution in renal impairment.

skill: First unprovoked seizure / driving restrictions and evaluation
stem: A 26-year-old had a witnessed two-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure while sitting at home. He is now fully recovered, has normal glucose and electrolytes and no intoxication, fever, trauma or focal deficit. CT head is unremarkable. He asks whether he may drive to work tomorrow because this was his first-ever seizure.
ask: What is the most appropriate discharge counselling and follow-up?
options: Permit immediate driving because a single seizure is not sufficient to diagnose epilepsy.
Prescribe lifelong antiseizure medication without further evaluation because recurrence is inevitable.
Arrange no follow-up because normal CT and electrolytes exclude a neurological cause of seizure.
Advise no driving pending fitness-to-drive assessment and arrange EEG, MRI and specialist review.
Recommend driving only on quiet roads because reduced traffic eliminates the risk of sudden recurrence.
explanations: A first unprovoked seizure carries recurrence risk and affects licensing fitness even before epilepsy is formally diagnosed. Immediate driving is unsafe.
Long-term antiseizure therapy depends on recurrence risk, EEG/MRI findings, patient preference and specialist assessment; it is not automatic after every first event.
A normal CT and routine blood tests do not exclude epilepsy or structural lesions better detected by MRI. Neurological follow-up remains necessary.

Correct: advise immediate cessation of driving, discuss Austroads and state licensing rules, provide seizure safety advice, and arrange outpatient EEG, MRI and neurology follow-up when medically stable.
Quiet roads do not prevent impaired awareness or loss of vehicle control during a recurrent seizure. Licensing standards apply regardless of route or driving frequency.
pearl: After a first unprovoked seizure, do not clear driving solely because CT and blood tests are normal; licensing standards are diagnosis- and risk-specific.
pivot: Persistent confusion, focal neurological deficit, status epilepticus or suspected CNS infection requires admission and urgent investigation rather than routine outpatient follow-up.

steps: Check safety
Exclude acute provoking causes, assess recovery and provide emergency return precautions.
Investigate
Arrange specialist-directed EEG and brain MRI, and clarify seizure semiology and witness account.
Counsel
Advise no driving, water/height safety, sleep regularity and avoidance of seizure triggers.
Follow up
Arrange neurology review to assess recurrence risk, treatment need and state licensing requirements.
management.safety: The duration of driving restriction varies by circumstances and licensing category; do not promise a fixed return date.
management.local: Epilepsy Action Australia January 2026 driving and epilepsy factsheet and Austroads fitness-to-drive standards.

skill: Malignant bowel obstruction / goals-concordant symptom and surgical assessment
stem: A 68-year-old with metastatic ovarian cancer and extensive peritoneal disease presents with repeated vomiting, abdominal distension and colicky pain. CT demonstrates multifocal small-bowel obstruction without free air or bowel ischaemia. She is stable and has previously expressed a strong preference for comfort-focused treatment over burdensome surgery. Her daughter requests an immediate laparotomy.
ask: What is the best next management approach?
options: Proceed to emergency laparotomy because all mechanical bowel obstructions require surgical correction.
Give only intravenous fluids and discharge once vomiting settles, without discussing future care goals.
Start high-volume oral laxatives because multifocal obstruction is best treated with rapid bowel emptying.
Ignore the patient's documented preferences because the next of kin has requested an operation.
Provide symptom control and urgent multidisciplinary review, aligning surgical options with patient goals.
explanations: Surgery may benefit selected patients, but multifocal malignant obstruction with extensive peritoneal disease often has limited operative benefit and substantial morbidity. Consent and goals matter.
Fluids alone do not adequately treat vomiting, pain, secretion burden or recurrent obstruction. Discharge without a coordinated plan risks distress and readmission.
High-volume laxatives can worsen distension and pain in complete mechanical obstruction. Bowel regimen choices depend on whether obstruction is partial, functional or complete.

A patient with decision-making capacity directs treatment decisions; family preferences do not automatically override informed wishes. Shared discussion can address concerns without ignoring autonomy.

Correct: assess reversible complications, relieve nausea, pain and secretions, consider decompression and palliative pharmacotherapy, and involve surgery and palliative care to evaluate interventions against prognosis and the patient's goals.
pearl: Malignant bowel obstruction needs both clinical assessment and goals-of-care discussion; neither automatic surgery nor abandonment is appropriate.
pivot: Peritonitis, perforation, ischaemia or uncontrolled shock would require immediate emergency surgical assessment even when care is otherwise palliative.

steps: Assess
Review CT, examination, hydration, electrolytes, pain, capacity and any signs of strangulation.
Relieve symptoms
Provide antiemetics, analgesia and appropriate decompression or antisecretory therapy guided by specialists.
Discuss options
Involve palliative care and surgery to explain realistic benefits and burdens of intervention.
Respect choices
Document informed patient goals, family communication and a coordinated symptom/crisis plan.
management.safety: Do not give aggressive laxatives for complete obstruction or automatically override a capable patient's informed treatment preferences.
management.local: NSW South Eastern Sydney LHD Medical Management of Malignant Bowel Obstruction guideline.

skill: Early fetal growth restriction / absent umbilical end-diastolic flow
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 30+2 weeks has a fetus with estimated weight at the third centile. Ultrasound shows absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, normal amniotic fluid and no structural anomaly. CTG is currently reassuring, BP is 122/78 mmHg and she reports normal fetal movements. Her local unit has no neonatal intensive care.
ask: What is the safest immediate care pathway?
options: Arrange urgent tertiary maternal fetal medicine assessment, surveillance and preterm birth preparation.
Reassure because a normal CTG today excludes placental insufficiency for the next several weeks.
Schedule routine growth ultrasound in four weeks without altering the place of antenatal care.
Induce labour immediately at the local hospital because Doppler abnormalities always require same-day birth.
Give oral aspirin as the sole treatment to restore umbilical end-diastolic blood flow.
explanations: Correct: absent umbilical end-diastolic flow at 30 weeks signals high-risk placental insufficiency. Urgent specialist review, repeated Dopplers/CTG and delivery planning at an appropriate neonatal centre are needed, with corticosteroids and magnesium considered if preterm birth is likely.
A single reassuring CTG reflects only current fetal status and does not negate elevated risk from abnormal Dopplers and marked growth restriction. Close surveillance is essential.
A four-week interval risks unrecognised fetal deterioration. Growth surveillance must be paired with much more frequent fetal wellbeing assessment when Dopplers are severely abnormal.
Delivery timing depends on serial fetal testing, gestation, maternal status and neonatal capacity. Automatic delivery at a unit without NICU can add avoidable prematurity risk.
Aspirin is used preventively in selected pregnancies at pre-eclampsia risk; it cannot reliably reverse established severe placental Doppler abnormalities.
pearl: Absent umbilical end-diastolic flow in early FGR requires urgent tertiary review even with a currently reassuring CTG.
pivot: An isolated constitutionally small fetus with normal Dopplers, growth velocity and wellbeing follows a lower-intensity surveillance pathway.

steps: Escalate
Contact maternal fetal medicine urgently and arrange transfer or shared care with a tertiary neonatal-capable centre.
Surveil
Repeat umbilical and other indicated Dopplers, CTG and maternal pre-eclampsia assessment.
Prepare
Discuss antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate if early delivery becomes likely.
Plan birth
Individualise timing and mode of delivery using fetal testing, gestation and maternal status.
management.safety: Do not use a single normal CTG to override severe abnormal Doppler findings or leave follow-up for weeks.
management.local: Queensland Maternal Fetal Medicine clinical prioritisation: absent/reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow is an urgent referral trigger.

skill: Stage II twin-to-twin transfusion / fetal laser referral
stem: A 25-year-old with monochorionic diamniotic twins is reviewed at 21 weeks. Ultrasound shows a deepest vertical pocket of 1.2 cm in one sac and 10 cm in the other. The donor twin's bladder is not visible, while both fetuses have cardiac activity and no hydrops. The family asks if repeated fluid drainage is the preferred definitive treatment.
ask: What management is most appropriate for this stage of disease?
options: Observe until 28 weeks because both twins remain alive and the recipient has no hydrops.
Refer urgently to a fetal therapy centre to assess fetoscopic laser ablation of placental vessels.
Deliver both twins immediately because donor oligohydramnios is irreversible without birth.
Prescribe maternal diuretics to lower the recipient sac volume without invasive intervention.
Arrange serial amnioreduction only because it corrects the abnormal placental vascular connections.
explanations: The absent donor bladder with oligo-polyhydramnios is at least Quintero stage II TTTS. Expectant observation alone risks progression and fetal loss.

Correct: stage II TTTS at 21 weeks warrants urgent tertiary fetal therapy evaluation. Fetoscopic laser ablation targets communicating placental vessels and is usually preferred over repeated drainage for early severe TTTS.
Delivery at 21 weeks would confer extreme prematurity and is not first-line while fetal therapy is potentially available. Counselling must consider prognosis and maternal risks.
Maternal diuretics do not correct placental vascular imbalance and may compromise maternal or placental circulation. They are not standard TTTS treatment.
Amnioreduction can relieve polyhydramnios in selected circumstances but does not interrupt the underlying placental anastomoses, so recurrence and fetal injury risks remain.
pearl: Absent donor bladder in monochorionic twins with oligohydramnios/polyhydramnios indicates at least stage II TTTS and prompts laser-centre referral.
pivot: Stage I TTTS with a visible donor bladder and stable cervical findings may sometimes be monitored closely in a specialist centre.

steps: Confirm stage
Repeat detailed monochorionic ultrasound, fetal bladders, fluid pockets, Dopplers and cervical assessment.
Refer
Contact an experienced fetal therapy centre urgently for counselling and laser suitability assessment.
Treat cause
Discuss fetoscopic laser ablation versus alternatives based on stage, anatomy and family goals.
Surveil
Continue post-treatment monitoring for recurrent TTTS, TAPS, growth and neurological complications.
management.safety: Do not delay fetal therapy referral for repeated amnioreduction or wait until hydrops develops.
management.local: NSW Health Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy guideline and Australian fetal therapy centre practice.

skill: Vitamin B12 deficiency with neurological deficits / parenteral replacement
stem: A 64-year-old vegetarian taking long-term metformin reports months of numb feet, unsteady walking and memory difficulty. Examination reveals impaired vibration and proprioception, brisk knee reflexes and a positive Romberg sign. Hb is 108 g/L, MCV 111 fL and vitamin B12 is markedly low. He asks whether folic acid tablets alone would reverse the problem.
ask: What is the most appropriate treatment priority?
options: Start folic acid alone because it corrects macrocytosis and therefore prevents neurological progression.
Wait for nerve conduction studies before giving any vitamins because neuropathy is not specific.
Begin prompt intramuscular vitamin B12 replacement and investigate the underlying deficiency cause.
Give high-dose iron alone because macrocytosis reflects reticulocyte production after occult bleeding.
Stop all neurological assessment because B12 treatment always reverses established cord damage completely.
explanations: Folate may improve anaemia while allowing B12-related neurological damage to progress. It is not a substitute for cobalamin replacement in symptomatic deficiency.
Nerve studies may help evaluate persistent or atypical symptoms, but clear neurological deficits and markedly low B12 warrant treatment without delay.

Correct: neurological involvement warrants prompt parenteral hydroxocobalamin loading, monitoring of clinical response and evaluation for pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, diet and medicine contributions.
Iron deficiency typically causes microcytosis rather than marked macrocytosis with posterior-column signs. Iron is indicated only if coexisting deficiency is confirmed.
Neurological improvement may be incomplete if deficiency has been prolonged. Ongoing examination and rehabilitation are important even after biochemical correction.
pearl: B12 deficiency with gait ataxia or proprioceptive loss needs urgent parenteral replacement; folate alone can mask anaemia while neuropathy progresses.
pivot: Mild asymptomatic dietary B12 deficiency without malabsorption may be treated orally with appropriate adherence and response monitoring.

steps: Treat
Begin intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading according to neurological-deficit protocol.
Investigate
Assess diet, metformin, pernicious anaemia, malabsorption and other causes of macrocytosis.
Monitor
Track neurological examination, FBC, B12 response and associated folate, iron or potassium issues.
Support recovery
Arrange gait safety, physiotherapy and appropriate long-term maintenance replacement.
management.safety: Do not give folate alone when B12 deficiency is suspected with neurological signs; irreversible deficits can result.
management.local: Australian Prescriber 2026 Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment, severe neurological deficiency requires intramuscular therapy.

skill: Primary hyperparathyroidism with osteoporosis / surgical indication
stem: A 62-year-old with repeatedly elevated corrected calcium of 2.78 mmol/L has inappropriately elevated PTH, normal renal function and no malignancy symptoms. Vitamin D is sufficient and urinary calcium does not suggest familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. DXA shows a lumbar T-score of −3.0 and she has sustained a low-trauma wrist fracture.
ask: What is the most appropriate next management decision?
options: Observe without further referral because calcium is below 3.0 mmol/L and she has no kidney stones.
Treat with vitamin D alone because the raised PTH is necessarily due to secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Order parathyroid scintigraphy as the diagnostic test before confirming the biochemical disorder.
Refer for endocrine surgical assessment because skeletal complications make parathyroidectomy appropriate.
Use lifelong high-dose loop diuretics because they cure the underlying excess parathyroid hormone secretion.
explanations: Primary hyperparathyroidism can cause important skeletal disease even when calcium is only mildly elevated. Osteoporosis and fragility fracture support intervention rather than indefinite observation.
Vitamin D deficiency has already been excluded, and calcium is high with inappropriately high PTH. Vitamin D alone will not cure autonomous parathyroid secretion.
Localisation imaging assists operative planning after biochemical diagnosis; it is not the primary diagnostic test for hyperparathyroidism.

Correct: confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism with osteoporosis and fragility fracture warrants endocrine/endocrine-surgery referral to discuss definitive parathyroidectomy and fracture-risk management.
Loop diuretics are not a curative long-term therapy and can cause dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities. Surgical treatment addresses the source of inappropriate PTH secretion.
pearl: Osteoporosis or fragility fracture is a clinically important reason to consider parathyroidectomy even without marked hypercalcaemia.
pivot: Mild asymptomatic disease without skeletal, renal or other surgical criteria may be monitored under an agreed endocrine surveillance plan.

steps: Confirm
Review repeated calcium, PTH, vitamin D, renal function and urinary calcium to exclude mimics.
Assess organs
Review DXA, fracture history and kidney stones or nephrocalcinosis.
Refer
Discuss endocrine surgical evaluation and shared decision-making about parathyroidectomy.
Protect bone
Optimise fracture prevention, falls risk and follow-up while definitive treatment is considered.
management.safety: Do not use parathyroid localisation imaging to establish the diagnosis before biochemical confirmation.
management.local: Queensland Health endocrine surgery prioritisation: primary hyperparathyroidism with severe osteoporosis or stones warrants specialist assessment.

skill: Painless visible haematuria on anticoagulant / malignancy investigation
stem: A 68-year-old former smoker taking apixaban for atrial fibrillation reports two episodes of painless red urine. Urine culture is negative, renal function is stable and he has no flank pain or fever. Haematuria stopped spontaneously after one day. He asks whether anticoagulation explains it and makes investigation unnecessary.
ask: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Attribute the bleeding to apixaban and reassure because spontaneous resolution excludes a tumour.
Repeat urine dipstick in six months and refer only if visible blood returns repeatedly.
Stop apixaban permanently without reviewing stroke risk because the urinary bleeding has ceased.
Prescribe antibiotics empirically because an occult infection is the commonest cause of painless haematuria.
Arrange prompt urological evaluation with cystoscopy and appropriate upper urinary tract imaging.
explanations: Anticoagulants may reveal bleeding from an underlying lesion; they do not exclude malignancy. Age, smoking and painless gross haematuria increase concern.
Intermittent visible haematuria is typical of some urothelial cancers. Waiting for recurrence can delay diagnosis and treatment.
Anticoagulant interruption requires balancing bleeding severity against embolic stroke risk. It does not replace investigation and should not be permanent by default.
Negative culture and absent infective symptoms make empirical antibiotics inappropriate. Even if infection coexists, persistent or high-risk visible haematuria still needs review.
Correct: organise timely urology referral for cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging, while assessing renal function, blood count and anticoagulation safety.
pearl: Visible painless haematuria in an older smoker needs urological investigation even when the patient takes anticoagulants.
pivot: Acute clot retention, heavy ongoing bleeding, anaemia or haemodynamic instability requires emergency stabilisation before outpatient cancer investigation.

steps: Assess stability
Review haemodynamic status, clot retention, haemoglobin, renal function and anticoagulant dose.
Exclude infection
Obtain urinalysis and culture and examine for stones or other relevant causes.
Investigate cancer
Refer promptly for cystoscopy and appropriate upper-tract imaging such as CT urography.
Coordinate
Manage anticoagulation based on bleeding severity and thromboembolic risk with treating clinicians.
management.safety: Do not dismiss visible haematuria as a harmless anticoagulant side effect or stop stroke-prevention treatment reflexively.
management.local: RACGP macroscopic haematuria assessment: urology referral, cystoscopy and upper tract imaging for high-risk presentations.

skill: Prolonged conjugated jaundice / urgent biliary atresia exclusion
stem: A thriving 24-day-old term infant remains jaundiced. Parents describe very pale putty-coloured stools and dark urine. Total bilirubin is 126 micromol/L, with conjugated bilirubin 58 micromol/L. An abdominal ultrasound requested by another clinician was reported as normal.
ask: What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Contact paediatric gastroenterology urgently for cholestasis assessment despite the reassuring abdominal ultrasound.
Repeat total bilirubin in four weeks and review only if the infant stops gaining weight.
Commence intensive phototherapy and defer specialist investigation until the total bilirubin concentration falls.
Label the condition breast-milk jaundice and advise a temporary switch to formula feeding.
Order a routine stool culture and wait for results before considering hepatobiliary referral.
explanations: Correct: acholic stools, dark urine and a markedly raised conjugated fraction suggest obstructive cholestasis, including biliary atresia. Urgent specialist evaluation is time-sensitive because early surgery improves outcomes; a normal ultrasound cannot exclude biliary atresia.
Weight gain does not exclude serious cholestasis. Waiting weeks risks missing the window for timely biliary atresia assessment and intervention.
Phototherapy treats significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not conjugated cholestasis. It would distract from evaluating biliary obstruction and associated liver dysfunction.
Breast-milk jaundice is predominantly unconjugated and a diagnosis of exclusion. Pale stools and dark urine are not typical reassuring features.
Routine stool culture does not investigate bile flow. Infectious causes may be evaluated alongside the urgent cholestasis work-up, not before referral.
pearl: Any acholic stool in a jaundiced infant warrants urgent biliary-atresia exclusion even when ultrasound appears normal.
pivot: An otherwise thriving infant with isolated unconjugated jaundice, normal stool colour and normal direct bilirubin follows a different pathway.

steps: Recognise
Confirm pale stools and dark urine; assess hydration, feeding, weight and hepatosplenomegaly.
Investigate
Check fractionated bilirubin, liver tests, INR and other tests guided by specialist advice.
Escalate
Call paediatric gastroenterology urgently; arrange expedited hepatobiliary evaluation and imaging.
Support
Address vitamin K/coagulopathy and nutritional needs under specialist guidance while awaiting diagnosis.
management.safety: Do not let a normal ultrasound or good weight gain delay assessment of possible biliary atresia.
management.local: RCH Melbourne: prolonged jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia or pale stools needs urgent gastroenterology discussion.

skill: IgA vasculitis / delayed renal involvement surveillance
stem: A 6-year-old has palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, transient ankle pain and a recent upper respiratory illness. She is well hydrated, normotensive and has a normal initial urine dipstick. Her abdominal examination is benign and she can walk comfortably.
ask: Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Discharge without urine surveillance because a normal initial dipstick excludes subsequent nephritis.
Arrange scheduled blood-pressure and urine checks over months, escalating if renal abnormalities develop.
Prescribe high-dose prednisolone routinely because it reliably prevents later IgA vasculitis nephritis.
Perform renal biopsy immediately despite normal urine testing and preserved kidney function today.
Start prophylactic antibiotics until the purpuric rash disappears to reduce renal complication risk.
explanations: Renal involvement can appear after the skin rash and may initially be silent. A single normal urinalysis cannot provide reliable long-term reassurance.

Correct: IgA vasculitis requires serial BP and urine monitoring even when initially uncomplicated. RCH suggests weekly checks for four weeks, fortnightly for the next eight weeks, then checks at six and twelve months if normal.
Corticosteroids may help selected severe abdominal or joint symptoms but do not reliably prevent nephritis. They are not indicated simply because purpura is present.
Biopsy is reserved for selected children with significant or persistent renal involvement, not normal BP and urine at first presentation.
IgA vasculitis is a small-vessel inflammatory condition; prophylactic antibiotics do not prevent its renal complications and add avoidable harms.
pearl: Kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis may be delayed and asymptomatic; BP plus urinalysis are central follow-up tests.
pivot: Macroscopic haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function or substantial proteinuria warrants earlier specialist involvement.

steps: Confirm
Review distribution of palpable purpura, joints, abdomen, testicles and vital signs.
Baseline
Document blood pressure and urinalysis; quantify protein and assess renal function if abnormal.
Monitor
Schedule weekly then fortnightly urine and BP reviews, with later six- and twelve-month checks.
Escalate
Seek paediatric or nephrology advice for hypertension, proteinuria, macroscopic haematuria or systemic complications.
management.safety: Never discharge IgA vasculitis without a reliable renal monitoring plan and clear red-flag advice.
management.local: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne IgA vasculitis guideline provides follow-up frequency and renal referral criteria.

skill: SGLT2-associated euglycaemic ketoacidosis / perioperative recognition
stem: A 59-year-old with type 2 diabetes takes empagliflozin and underwent elective bowel surgery yesterday after taking the drug until admission. She is tachypnoeic, nauseated and dehydrated. Venous pH is 7.18, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L and glucose 10.4 mmol/L.
ask: What is the safest immediate treatment approach?
options: Administer subcutaneous correction insulin alone because glucose is below the usual DKA diagnostic threshold.
Give intravenous bicarbonate first and continue empagliflozin to prevent postoperative hyperglycaemia.
Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and initiate monitored DKA treatment with insulin, fluids and glucose as needed.
Treat postoperative nausea symptomatically and repeat ketones only if glucose rises above 20 mmol/L.
Restrict intravenous fluids and delay insulin until serum glucose becomes markedly elevated overnight.
explanations: Glucose can be normal or only modestly elevated in SGLT2-associated DKA. Correction-only subcutaneous insulin will not adequately suppress ketogenesis in significant acidosis.
Routine bicarbonate is not first-line DKA treatment at this pH. Continuing the SGLT2 inhibitor prolongs the pharmacological driver of ketosis.

Correct: this is euglycaemic DKA. Stop empagliflozin, begin a monitored DKA protocol with IV insulin, isotonic fluids, potassium surveillance and dextrose to permit ongoing insulin despite near-normal glucose.
Treating nausea without correcting ketoacidosis delays resuscitation. Waiting for hyperglycaemia misses the defining danger of SGLT2-related euglycaemic DKA.
Fluid restriction is inappropriate in a dehydrated patient unless a specific contraindication exists. Insulin is required to stop ketone generation even with modest glycaemia.
pearl: Always check ketones and acid-base status in an unwell SGLT2 user; a glucose of 10 mmol/L does not exclude DKA.
pivot: Isolated starvation ketosis typically causes less severe acidosis; assess the entire biochemical and clinical context.

steps: Stabilise
Assess ABC, volume status, venous blood gas, glucose, ketones, electrolytes and ECG.
Stop trigger
Withhold empagliflozin and identify fasting, surgery, infection or insulin deficiency.
Treat DKA
Give protocolised IV fluids and insulin with dextrose and potassium management as indicated.
Monitor
Track ketone clearance, anion gap, glucose, potassium and fluid balance until resolution.
management.safety: Never wait for marked hyperglycaemia before treating severe ketonaemic acidosis in an SGLT2 user.
management.local: RACGP Australian guidance: SGLT2-related DKA may have only modest hyperglycaemia; withhold during illness, fasting and before surgery.

skill: Congenital CMV / diagnostic PCR window after failed hearing screen
stem: A 12-day-old term baby fails a repeat newborn hearing screen on the left. Pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated, and the infant has no rash, jaundice or microcephaly. The parents ask whether a viral cause can be confirmed now and what happens if testing is delayed.
ask: Which investigation plan is most appropriate?
options: Arrange maternal CMV IgG testing at six weeks and diagnose congenital infection if it is positive.
Request neonatal CMV IgM alone because positive serology definitively distinguishes congenital from acquired infection.
Wait until the routine three-month audiology appointment before collecting a CMV specimen for diagnosis.
Collect neonatal saliva or urine CMV PCR promptly within 21 days, confirming positive saliva in urine.
Order brain MRI as the initial diagnostic test and perform viral PCR only if imaging is abnormal.
explanations: Maternal IgG commonly indicates past exposure and cannot confirm congenital infection in the infant. Timing and neonatal virological testing are essential.
Neonatal CMV serology lacks sufficient sensitivity and specificity to establish congenital infection. A negative IgM does not rule it out.
After day 21, a positive viral test cannot reliably distinguish congenital infection from postnatally acquired CMV without stored early samples.

Correct: collect saliva or urine PCR before 21 days of life; confirm a positive saliva test with urine PCR to avoid contamination from breast milk. Prompt audiology and specialist assessment should follow.
MRI helps assess CNS involvement after suspected or confirmed disease but does not replace timely PCR confirmation of congenital CMV.
pearl: Congenital CMV is best confirmed by neonatal saliva or urine PCR collected during the first 21 days.
pivot: Positive PCR obtained after 21 days needs careful interpretation or retrospective dried-blood-spot evaluation if available.

steps: Test now
Collect saliva or urine CMV PCR immediately while still within the congenital diagnostic window.
Confirm
Confirm positive saliva PCR on urine and assess other congenital infection findings.
Stage disease
Arrange audiology, examination, blood counts, liver tests, ophthalmology and imaging when indicated.
Refer
Discuss hearing loss and treatment eligibility promptly with paediatric infectious diseases and audiology.
management.safety: Do not defer virological sampling until the diagnostic window closes, even in a well-appearing infant.
management.local: Children's Health Queensland congenital CMV treatment guideline: diagnosis requires samples within the first 21 days.

skill: Macrolide-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium / resistance-guided sequential therapy
stem: A 25-year-old man has persistent urethral discomfort after negative gonorrhoea and chlamydia NAATs. Mycoplasma genitalium NAAT is positive, with a detected macrolide-resistance mutation. He is haemodynamically well, has no testicular pain, and has not received treatment for this episode.
ask: Which regimen best follows Australian resistance-guided guidance?
options: Give azithromycin 1 g once, without follow-up, because it remains effective against resistant strains.
Treat with ceftriaxone alone and repeat the gonorrhoea test if urethral symptoms persist.
Use doxycycline for seven days and then high-dose azithromycin despite proven macrolide resistance.
Prescribe metronidazole for seven days and defer any partner management until symptoms recur.
Give doxycycline for seven days followed by moxifloxacin for seven days after safety assessment.
explanations: Macrolide resistance predicts poor azithromycin response. A single-dose regimen also risks further selection of resistance and is not the recommended approach.
Ceftriaxone targets gonorrhoea, which has tested negative, and does not reliably eradicate Mycoplasma genitalium.
Sequential doxycycline followed by extended azithromycin is used for susceptible infections; a resistance mutation changes the second agent.
Metronidazole does not treat Mycoplasma genitalium. Partner assessment and transmission counselling should not be deferred.

Correct: Australian STI guidance recommends doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for seven days, then moxifloxacin 400 mg daily for seven days for macrolide-resistant infection, subject to contraindications and interactions.
pearl: Use resistance testing where available: doxycycline lowers bacterial load before the targeted second antibiotic.
pivot: Pregnancy, fluoroquinolone contraindications, treatment failure or complicated PID require specialist-tailored alternatives.

steps: Confirm
Review NAAT and macrolide-resistance result; assess symptoms, sexual exposures and co-infections.
Treat
Use sequential doxycycline then moxifloxacin per current Australian STI guidance and contraindications.
Prevent
Advise abstinence until treatment completion and appropriate partner testing or treatment advice.
Review
Arrange recommended test-of-cure timing and specialist input for persistence or treatment intolerance.
management.safety: Check pregnancy status when relevant and assess QT prolongation, tendon risk and drug interactions before moxifloxacin.
management.local: STI Guidelines Australia: macrolide-resistant M. genitalium is treated with sequential doxycycline and moxifloxacin.

skill: Potential HIV exposure / timely non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis
stem: A 24-year-old presents 38 hours after condomless receptive anal intercourse with a partner newly confirmed to have HIV. He does not take PrEP, has no known renal disease, and his rapid baseline HIV test is negative. The partner's viral load is not yet available.
ask: What is the most appropriate management now?
options: Assess exposure risk and start indicated HIV PEP immediately, arranging baseline tests and follow-up.
Defer antiretroviral prophylaxis until the source viral-load result confirms ongoing infectiousness.
Offer daily HIV PrEP alone because the exposure occurred more than twenty-four hours ago.
Repeat a rapid HIV test at seven days and initiate PEP only if seroconversion occurs.
Provide empirical antibiotics for common STIs and avoid HIV-specific prevention pending specialist review.
explanations: Correct: 38 hours is within the 72-hour PEP window. A significant exposure warrants urgent assessment and initiation of a recommended 28-day regimen when indicated; do not delay for source viral load or routine baseline results.
Waiting for a source viral load may lose the time-sensitive prophylaxis opportunity. A reliably undetectable source viral load could change risk assessment, but it is not established here.
PrEP prevents future acquisition when taken appropriately; it is not a substitute for PEP after a significant exposure in someone not already protected.
PEP works by preventing establishment of infection after exposure, not treating established seroconversion. A negative initial test is expected soon after exposure.
STI screening and prevention are important adjuncts, but antibiotics do not prevent HIV acquisition and should not replace urgent PEP assessment.
