pearl: HIV PEP is most effective when started promptly, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure.
pivot: If the source has a reliably sustained undetectable viral load, exposure-risk assessment may change; verify rather than assume.

steps: Assess
Clarify timing, type of exposure, source HIV status, current PrEP use and pregnancy potential.
Start
Commence a recommended 28-day PEP regimen promptly when risk assessment indicates.
Screen
Arrange baseline HIV, hepatitis B/C, STI testing and renal function without delaying treatment.
Follow up
Support adherence, arrange repeat testing per local protocol and discuss transition to PrEP if ongoing risk.
management.safety: Do not wait for source viral-load testing when indicated PEP is time-critical and the result is unavailable.
management.local: ASHM Australian PEP clinical tool: begin as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours and no later than 72 hours.

skill: Denosumab cessation / rebound vertebral fracture prevention
stem: A 75-year-old with osteoporosis has received denosumab every six months for four years without fractures. Her last injection was six months ago. She wishes to stop because she feels well, and asks whether she can take a drug holiday as her friend did with alendronate.
ask: What is the best response and treatment plan?
options: Agree to a twelve-month drug holiday and reassess bone density only if back pain develops.
Explain rebound fracture risk and arrange uninterrupted therapy or planned bisphosphonate transition.
Replace denosumab with calcium alone because bone density has improved since treatment began.
Reduce denosumab to yearly injections so the antiresorptive effect wears off more gradually.
Stop treatment immediately and use a short prednisolone course to prevent rebound bone turnover.
explanations: Bisphosphonate holidays cannot be extrapolated to denosumab. Rapid reversal of its effect can cause multiple vertebral fractures even in previously stable patients.
Correct: denosumab should not be interrupted without a plan. If stopping, arrange a timely bisphosphonate transition, usually for at least twelve months, with specialist input when appropriate.
Calcium and vitamin D sufficiency support bone health but do not adequately prevent denosumab-withdrawal rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures.
Denosumab is intended at six-month intervals. Extending to annual dosing creates an unprotected period rather than a safe taper.
Glucocorticoids increase skeletal fragility and have no role in preventing denosumab rebound; they could worsen fracture risk.
pearl: Denosumab is not a drug-holiday medication; plan antiresorptive cover before stopping.
pivot: A bisphosphonate holiday may be considered in selected low-risk patients after prolonged bisphosphonate therapy, not after denosumab.

steps: Review
Assess fracture history, current BMD, renal function, calcium, vitamin D and treatment goals.
Continue
Arrange the next denosumab dose on schedule if ongoing treatment is chosen.
Transition
If stopping, plan bisphosphonate therapy for at least twelve months with an appropriate start date.
Monitor
Reassess fractures, symptoms, adherence and BMD; consider specialist advice for high-risk patients.
management.safety: Never simply omit the next denosumab injection without a documented follow-on antiresorptive strategy.
management.local: 2024 RACGP–Healthy Bones Australia osteoporosis guideline: avoid interruption; transition to bisphosphonate for at least twelve months if ceased.

skill: Post-treatment CIN3 surveillance / HPV16-positive test of cure
stem: A 36-year-old underwent excisional treatment for histologically confirmed CIN3 twelve months ago. Her planned test of cure now shows oncogenic HPV type 16 detected, while reflex liquid-based cytology reports no intraepithelial lesion. She has no abnormal bleeding.
ask: Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Return to routine five-yearly HPV screening because the cytology is currently negative.
Repeat HPV testing in twelve months without referral because treatment removes all residual risk.
Refer for colposcopy despite negative cytology because HPV16 is detected during test of cure.
Repeat the excisional procedure immediately without examining the cervix or reviewing histology.
Use topical vaginal oestrogen and repeat cytology after symptoms of atrophy have resolved.
explanations: A negative cytology result does not override detection of HPV16 after treatment for high-grade disease. Routine screening requires documented clearance through the test-of-cure pathway.
Annual surveillance without colposcopy is not the recommended response to HPV16 positivity during post-treatment test of cure.
Correct: oncogenic HPV16/18 positivity during test of cure triggers colposcopic assessment regardless of reflex cytology. Subsequent management depends on colposcopic and histological findings.
Repeat excision may be required for proven recurrent high-grade lesions, but proceeding without assessment risks unnecessary cervical morbidity.
Atrophic changes can affect cytology interpretation but do not explain away a positive HPV16 result after treatment for CIN3.
pearl: HPV16 or HPV18 detected during post-treatment test of cure warrants colposcopy even when cytology is negative.
pivot: Two consecutive negative annual co-tests after treatment permit return to routine screening under the Australian pathway.

steps: Verify
Review prior CIN3 pathology, excision margins and timing of post-treatment co-testing.
Refer
Arrange colposcopy for HPV16 positivity irrespective of negative liquid-based cytology.
Evaluate
Use directed examination and biopsy when indicated rather than empirical repeat excision.
Track
Document results and schedule surveillance according to the national test-of-cure algorithm.
management.safety: Do not falsely reassure based on negative cytology when high-risk HPV16 persists after high-grade cervical disease.
management.local: Metro North Queensland Health: HPV16/18 positivity at any point during test of cure requires colposcopy.

skill: Functional neurological weakness / positive diagnosis and communication
stem: A 28-year-old develops intermittent left-leg weakness after a stressful hospital admission. MRI brain and spine show no structural explanation. Examination reveals reduced voluntary hip extension, but normal automatic extension when the opposite hip flexes against resistance (positive Hoover sign). Reflexes and plantar responses are normal.
ask: What is the best diagnostic and management approach?
options: Conclude malingering because weakness improves during distraction and offer no further follow-up.
Explain that normal imaging proves there is no illness and discharge without rehabilitation.
Order serial spinal MRI indefinitely because functional neurological disorder requires excluding every disease.
Make a positive FND diagnosis, explain the signs respectfully and arrange targeted rehabilitation.
Commence long-term antipsychotic treatment because functional symptoms represent a psychotic illness.
explanations: Inconsistency on examination is a positive sign of functional neurological disorder, not proof of conscious fabrication. Accusations damage therapeutic engagement.
Symptoms are genuine and can cause substantial disability despite normal structural imaging. Clear explanation and active treatment are more helpful than dismissal.
FND is diagnosed through positive clinical signs, while investigations are tailored to red flags. Endless exclusionary testing can reinforce uncertainty and delay recovery.

Correct: Hoover sign supports a positive functional weakness diagnosis. Explain the finding non-judgementally, screen for coexisting neurological disease, and refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and psychological support as appropriate.
FND is not synonymous with psychosis. Antipsychotics have no routine role unless a separate indication is present.
pearl: Functional neurological disorder is a positive clinical diagnosis, not simply normal scans or an accusation of feigning.
pivot: New objective focal signs, progressive deficits or atypical features warrant reconsideration for coexisting neurological pathology.

steps: Demonstrate
Document reproducible positive signs such as Hoover sign and assess for neurological red flags.
Explain
Describe altered nervous-system functioning as real and potentially reversible, using the positive findings.
Treat
Arrange FND-informed physiotherapy, graded activity and targeted psychological input when useful.
Review
Monitor function, mental health, diagnostic evolution and any new neurological symptoms.
management.safety: Never equate a positive Hoover sign with malingering or use normal imaging alone to dismiss symptoms.
management.local: Australian Journal of General Practice 2025: FND should be diagnosed using positive signs and treated as genuine dysfunction.

skill: Hepatitis B needlestick / HBIG and vaccine in susceptible worker
stem: A junior doctor sustains a hollow-bore needlestick while taking blood from a patient known to be hepatitis B surface-antigen positive. The injury occurred one hour ago. The doctor never completed hepatitis B vaccination and has no documented protective anti-HBs response.
ask: What is the most appropriate immediate prevention plan?
options: Clean the wound and wait for the source patient's hepatitis B viral load before offering prophylaxis.
Give hepatitis B vaccine alone and omit immunoglobulin because the doctor is a healthcare worker.
Prescribe tenofovir for twenty-eight days as the standard sole hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis.
Arrange HCV prophylaxis instead because hepatitis B immunoglobulin has no role after needlestick injury.
Provide prompt hepatitis B immunoglobulin plus vaccination and occupational-exposure follow-up.
explanations: The source is known HBsAg positive and the worker is susceptible. Delaying prophylaxis for viral-load testing risks preventable infection.
Vaccination establishes longer-term immunity but does not provide the immediate passive protection required for this significant exposure.
Antiretroviral HIV PEP regimens are not the standard hepatitis B prevention pathway; HBIG and vaccination are indicated in susceptible contacts.
There is no established HCV post-exposure prophylaxis. The known hepatitis B risk must be addressed directly.

Correct: provide wound first aid, report the incident, administer HBIG promptly (preferably within 72 hours) plus hepatitis B vaccine at a separate site, and arrange completion of vaccination and serological follow-up.
pearl: After a significant HBsAg-positive needlestick, susceptible staff need passive and active hepatitis B protection promptly.
pivot: A worker with a documented protective post-vaccination anti-HBs response generally does not require HBIG for this exposure.

steps: First aid
Wash the puncture with soap and water; document and report the exposure immediately.
Risk assess
Confirm source HBsAg status and the worker's vaccine and anti-HBs history; obtain baseline tests.
Prevent
Give HBIG and initiate hepatitis B vaccination promptly according to the exposure protocol.
Follow up
Complete vaccine series, check post-vaccine response and arrange occupational health surveillance.
management.safety: Do not delay HBIG in a susceptible person after significant exposure to known HBsAg-positive blood.
management.local: Queensland Health occupational-exposure guidance: assess urgently and start indicated hepatitis B PEP within 72 hours.

skill: Functional asplenia / meningococcal vaccination risk-group schedule
stem: A 19-year-old university student with sickle cell disease and functional asplenia attends a preventive health visit. She completed routine childhood vaccinations but has no documented meningococcal B vaccination and no risk-group meningococcal booster plan. She will be living in residential college.
ask: What is the most appropriate vaccination advice?
options: Arrange risk-group MenACWY and MenB vaccination with recommended booster planning and record review.
Rely on her routine childhood MenACWY dose because asplenia does not increase meningococcal risk.
Administer pneumococcal vaccine alone because it protects against all invasive encapsulated bacterial infections.
Offer a single meningococcal B dose without boosters because the risk ends after adolescence.
Defer meningococcal vaccination until splenectomy is performed because functional asplenia is not relevant.
explanations: Correct: functional asplenia increases invasive meningococcal disease risk. The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends both MenACWY and MenB primary courses with risk-group boosters, tailored to prior doses and age.
Routine adolescent MenACWY vaccination does not replace special-risk recommendations; the patient's functional asplenia persists throughout life.
Pneumococcal protection is important in asplenia but does not protect against meningococcal serogroups. A broader encapsulated-organism vaccination review is needed.
MenB primary dosing and boosters vary by risk group. A single unplanned dose may leave a high-risk person incompletely protected.
Functional asplenia from sickle cell disease carries infection risk even without surgical splenectomy, so immunisation should not wait.
pearl: Asplenia requires special-risk meningococcal schedules, including both MenACWY and MenB, not just routine adolescent doses.
pivot: An otherwise healthy student in residential accommodation is also recommended meningococcal protection, but booster indications differ.

steps: Review
Confirm vaccination record, sickle cell complications, immune status and prior MenACWY/MenB doses.
Vaccinate
Arrange catch-up or primary MenACWY and MenB courses per current special-risk guidance.
Boost
Schedule indicated MenACWY and MenB booster doses for ongoing asplenia risk.
Prevent
Review pneumococcal, influenza and other vaccines and provide fever/sepsis emergency advice.
management.safety: Fever in a person with asplenia can represent rapidly progressive sepsis; vaccination does not eliminate the need for urgent assessment.
management.local: Australian Immunisation Handbook: asplenia is a special-risk condition requiring MenACWY and MenB courses and boosters.

skill: Gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis / urgent biliary drainage
stem: A 66-year-old presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, fever and jaundice. Lipase is six times the upper limit of normal, bilirubin is 92 micromol/L and ultrasound shows gallstones with a dilated common bile duct. BP is 88/54 mmHg despite initial fluid resuscitation.
ask: What is the most appropriate definitive management priority alongside sepsis treatment?
options: Schedule outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy once bilirubin has normalised without further intervention.
Arrange urgent ERCP for biliary decompression while resuscitating and giving intravenous antibiotics.
Provide analgesia and observe for spontaneous passage because pancreatitis makes endoscopy contraindicated.
Commence oral ursodeoxycholic acid and repeat ultrasound after seven days of inpatient observation.
Perform immediate elective cholecystectomy before treating sepsis because the gallbladder is the source.
explanations: Definitive gallbladder removal is important after recovery, but outpatient surgery alone does not relieve infected obstructed ducts during cholangitis and shock.

Correct: pancreatitis with obstructive jaundice, fever and shock suggests concomitant acute cholangitis. Resuscitate, obtain cultures, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent biliary drainage, usually ERCP, with specialist support.
Observation alone risks worsening septic shock and organ failure when infected biliary obstruction is suspected. Early ERCP is specifically indicated with cholangitis.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is not an acute source-control treatment for infected biliary obstruction and should not delay drainage.
Cholecystectomy may follow stabilisation, but immediate gallbladder surgery does not reliably decompress the common bile duct and is unsafe before shock management.
pearl: Routine early ERCP is not indicated for uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis; concomitant cholangitis changes the priority.
pivot: If pancreatitis occurs without cholangitis or persistent obstruction, supportive care and appropriately timed cholecystectomy take precedence.

steps: Resuscitate
Manage sepsis, ABC, IV access, fluids, cultures, lactate and close haemodynamic monitoring.
Treat infection
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics according to local biliary-sepsis guidance and organ function.
Drain
Urgently discuss ERCP or alternative biliary drainage with gastroenterology and surgery.
Prevent recurrence
After stabilisation, plan definitive gallstone management and assess complications of pancreatitis.
management.safety: Do not defer biliary source control in a patient with shock, jaundice and suspected acute cholangitis.
management.local: Queensland Health classifies gallstones with cholangitis as an emergency; 2025 International Association of Pancreatology guidance supports early ERCP when cholangitis complicates biliary pancreatitis.

skill: Very severe intrahepatic cholestasis / risk stratification by peak bile acids
stem: A 34-year-old at 35+1 weeks has intense nocturnal itching of her palms and soles without rash. Her non-fasting total bile acids are 126 micromol/L and ALT is mildly elevated. BP and platelet count are normal, and fetal growth is appropriate. She asks whether improving itching means she can wait until 40 weeks.
ask: Which plan best addresses maternal and fetal risk?
options: Use antihistamines alone and await spontaneous labour because fetal risk tracks maternal itching severity.
Repeat bile acids at 39 weeks and arrange delivery only if transaminases rise above 500 U/L.
Arrange urgent specialist birth planning for very severe ICP, discussing delivery around 35–36 weeks.
Treat with topical corticosteroids and continue routine care because absent rash excludes cholestasis.
Schedule an elective caesarean at 40 weeks because the delivery mode, not timing, prevents stillbirth.
explanations: Maternal symptom relief does not reliably indicate reduced fetal risk. Antihistamines may help sleep but do not address the very high bile-acid-associated risk.
Waiting until 39 weeks is unsafe with peak bile acids above 100 micromol/L. ALT alone is not the main determinant of fetal risk.

Correct: bile acids at or above 100 micromol/L define very severe ICP with increased stillbirth risk from around 35 weeks. Urgent senior obstetric discussion should address timing of birth, neonatal implications and maternal treatment.
ICP typically presents with pruritus without primary rash; lack of rash supports rather than excludes the diagnosis. Topical steroids do not manage bile-acid-associated risk.
Caesarean is not automatically required for ICP. Timing and individual obstetric indications guide induction versus caesarean, with shared decision-making.
pearl: In ICP, peak bile acids—not itch intensity or falling levels alone—are key to fetal risk stratification.
pivot: Pruritus with normal bile acids warrants reassessment if symptoms persist, rather than diagnosing very severe ICP without biochemical evidence.

steps: Confirm
Review bile acids, liver tests, blood pressure, platelets and differential diagnoses of pruritus.
Risk stratify
Classify peak bile acids above 100 micromol/L as very severe and discuss fetal risk.
Plan birth
Urgently involve senior obstetrics for individualised delivery timing, often around 35–36 weeks.
Support
Offer ursodeoxycholic acid for symptoms, discuss fetal surveillance limits and arrange postpartum liver review.
management.safety: Do not reassure based solely on improved itching or a lower repeat bile-acid result after a peak above 100.
management.local: SOMANZ 2023 consensus: peak bile acids ≥100 micromol/L indicate very severe ICP with higher stillbirth risk from 35 weeks.

skill: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis / asymptomatic anterior uveitis screening
stem: A 5-year-old girl is diagnosed with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis after three months of painless knee swelling and morning stiffness. ANA is positive. Her eyes look normal, she has no photophobia and visual acuity is age appropriate.
ask: What is the best preventive management step?
options: Wait for red eyes or visual complaints before arranging ophthalmology because asymptomatic disease is unlikely.
Order yearly retinal photography alone because uveitis is usually visible on a routine fundus image.
Prescribe prophylactic topical steroid drops without an eye examination to prevent silent inflammation.
Arrange regular slit-lamp ophthalmology screening even though she has no ocular symptoms.
Use a normal school vision screen to exclude anterior uveitis and avoid additional appointments.
explanations: Chronic anterior uveitis associated with JIA can be entirely asymptomatic until complications occur. Symptom-triggered review misses preventable visual damage.
Fundus photographs do not reliably detect anterior chamber inflammation. Slit-lamp examination is the appropriate screening method.
Empirical steroid drops without a diagnosis can cause ocular hypertension, cataract and infection risk; treatment is guided by ophthalmology.
Correct: children with JIA need regular slit-lamp assessments, with frequency based on age, JIA subtype, ANA status and duration. Early detection prevents cataract, glaucoma and vision loss.
Normal visual acuity and external appearance cannot rule out silent anterior uveitis; school screening is insufficient.
pearl: JIA-associated anterior uveitis can be silent; slit-lamp screening is essential even with normal-looking eyes.
pivot: Painful red photophobic eyes may suggest acute uveitis and require urgent ophthalmology review rather than routine screening.

steps: Risk assess
Document JIA subtype, age at onset, ANA status and any ocular symptoms.
Refer
Arrange baseline ophthalmology slit-lamp assessment and an individualised screening schedule.
Coordinate
Communicate with paediatric rheumatology about systemic disease and any uveitis therapy.
Educate
Explain silent visual risk and the importance of attendance despite no eye complaints.
management.safety: Do not wait for eye redness or reduced visual acuity before screening a child with JIA.
management.local: Sydney Children's Hospitals Network: all children with JIA require regular slit-lamp ophthalmology checks for often silent uveitis.

skill: Clozapine gastrointestinal hypomotility / obstruction red flags
stem: A 39-year-old with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine for five months. He reports no bowel motion for six days, progressive abdominal distension, colicky pain and repeated vomiting. He is tachycardic and looks unwell. His carer says constipation has been dismissed as a minor side effect.
ask: What is the safest immediate response?
options: Add fibre supplements and encourage exercise at home while continuing clozapine unchanged for a week.
Prescribe an oral bulk-forming laxative and arrange review only after normal bowel movements resume.
Reassure that clozapine constipation is harmless unless the absolute neutrophil count becomes low.
Increase clozapine to control agitation and delay abdominal imaging until psychotic symptoms stabilise.
Arrange emergency medical and surgical assessment for possible ileus or obstruction and review clozapine.
explanations: Fibre and exercise may help uncomplicated constipation, but vomiting, distension and pain indicate possible life-threatening hypomotility or obstruction requiring urgent assessment.
Bulk-forming agents can worsen obstruction when gut transit is impaired. This patient needs immediate examination and escalation, not an outpatient laxative trial.
Clozapine gastrointestinal hypomotility is independent of agranulocytosis and can be fatal. Normal neutrophils do not make abdominal red flags safe.
Increasing an anticholinergic medication may worsen hypomotility. Psychiatric stability is important but cannot supersede emergency abdominal assessment.

Correct: severe clozapine-associated gastrointestinal hypomotility can cause ileus, obstruction, ischaemia or perforation. Arrange emergency evaluation, imaging, fluids and surgical input, with psychiatric consultation about clozapine management.
pearl: Clozapine constipation is potentially fatal; vomiting, distension and persistent abdominal pain are emergency warning signs.
pivot: Uncomplicated constipation without red flags needs proactive bowel monitoring and appropriate non-bulk laxative treatment.

steps: Recognise
Assess abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, bowel motions, vital signs and signs of sepsis.
Escalate
Arrange urgent emergency, medical and surgical review; obtain imaging and laboratory assessment.
Treat
Manage suspected obstruction with IV fluids, bowel rest and specialist-directed interventions.
Prevent
Coordinate clozapine review and a documented bowel monitoring and laxative prevention plan.
management.safety: Never manage clozapine-related vomiting and abdominal distension as routine constipation in the community.
management.local: NSW Health clozapine guidance: abdominal distension, vomiting or sustained moderate-severe pain require immediate medical assessment.

skill: Adrenal crisis / immediate parenteral stress-dose hydrocortisone
stem: An 8-year-old with known primary adrenal insufficiency develops gastroenteritis and has vomited three times, including her usual oral hydrocortisone. She is lethargic, hypotensive and hypoglycaemic at 2.7 mmol/L. Her parents have brought the emergency hydrocortisone kit but have not administered it.
ask: What should be prioritised immediately?
options: Give IM or IV stress-dose hydrocortisone without delay alongside glucose and fluid resuscitation.
Repeat the usual oral hydrocortisone dose and reassess only if vomiting stops completely.
Await a morning serum cortisol result before administering steroids to preserve diagnostic accuracy.
Treat dehydration with oral rehydration alone because hypotension is expected with gastroenteritis.
Start a mineralocorticoid tablet first and defer glucocorticoid treatment until potassium is measured.
explanations: Correct: this is suspected adrenal crisis with vomiting, hypotension and hypoglycaemia. Give emergency parenteral hydrocortisone immediately (RCH age 3–12 initial 50 mg), treat hypoglycaemia and resuscitate with appropriate IV fluids.
Vomiting makes oral absorption unreliable. A routine replacement dose is insufficient during serious physiological stress and risks progression to shock.
Adrenal crisis is a clinical emergency. Blood can be collected if it does not delay treatment, but cortisol testing is not required before lifesaving steroids.
Oral rehydration is inadequate for a shocked, hypoglycaemic child unable to tolerate oral medication. Parenteral resuscitation is necessary.
Hydrocortisone supplies essential glucocorticoid activity and has mineralocorticoid effects at stress doses. Mineralocorticoid tablets are not the first rescue treatment.
pearl: Vomiting in a child with adrenal insufficiency can rapidly make oral replacement ineffective; use emergency parenteral hydrocortisone.
pivot: A well child with mild intercurrent illness who retains oral medication may use an agreed oral sick-day dosing plan.

steps: Recognise
Assess ABC, shock, hydration, blood glucose, electrolytes and known adrenal insufficiency.
Replace
Give age-appropriate IM or IV emergency hydrocortisone immediately; do not await laboratory results.
Resuscitate
Correct hypoglycaemia and give IV isotonic fluids with close haemodynamic reassessment.
Continue
Admit for ongoing stress dosing, trigger treatment and education on emergency injection use.
management.safety: Never delay hydrocortisone in suspected adrenal crisis to obtain confirmatory cortisol testing.
management.local: RCH Melbourne adrenal crisis guideline: children aged 3–12 require initial 50 mg IM/IV hydrocortisone and ongoing stress dosing.

skill: Acute rheumatic fever / long-term secondary prophylaxis
stem: A 13-year-old from a remote community is diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever after migratory large-joint arthritis, fever, elevated inflammatory markers and evidence of recent group A streptococcal infection. Echocardiography identifies mild mitral regurgitation. Symptoms improve with treatment and the family asks whether antibiotics can now stop.
ask: What is the most appropriate longer-term prevention strategy?
options: Give one oral antibiotic course and stop when arthritis resolves because recurrence is uncommon.
Arrange regular intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin secondary prophylaxis with register-supported follow-up.
Prescribe antibiotics only during future sore throats and repeat echocardiography if symptoms recur.
Use daily anti-inflammatory medication indefinitely instead of antibiotics to prevent further valve injury.
Recommend early valve surgery despite mild regurgitation because prophylaxis cannot prevent recurrence.
explanations: A single course treats active streptococcal infection but does not prevent subsequent group A streptococcal exposures and recurrent rheumatic fever.

Correct: long-term secondary prophylaxis, commonly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days, reduces recurrence and further valvular damage. Duration depends on age, severity of carditis, risk and specialist review.
Symptom-triggered antibiotics miss asymptomatic streptococcal infections and do not reliably prevent recurrence. Scheduled secondary prevention is required.
Anti-inflammatory therapy treats acute symptoms but does not prevent immune responses to subsequent streptococcal infection or progressive rheumatic heart disease.
Valve surgery is reserved for selected severe structural complications. Mild regurgitation calls for surveillance and secondary prevention rather than immediate operation.
pearl: Acute rheumatic fever requires long-term secondary penicillin prophylaxis even after fever and arthritis settle.
pivot: Duration of prophylaxis varies by carditis and residual valve disease; specialist echocardiographic review precedes cessation.

steps: Treat acute
Complete eradication therapy and manage arthritis or carditis with specialist input.
Prevent
Begin scheduled intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin secondary prophylaxis.
Coordinate
Enrol in an RHD register or equivalent system for recall and adherence support.
Monitor
Arrange periodic echocardiography, dental care, education and review of prophylaxis duration.
management.safety: Stopping prophylaxis because acute symptoms resolve exposes the patient to recurrent rheumatic fever and cumulative valve injury.
management.local: RHD Australia/Menzies: regular IM benzathine benzylpenicillin every 21–28 days is preferred secondary prevention.

skill: GBS urinary tract infection / antenatal treatment and intrapartum prophylaxis
stem: A 29-year-old at 26 weeks' gestation reports dysuria and frequency. Urine culture grows group B Streptococcus at 10^5 CFU/mL, susceptible to penicillin. She is afebrile with no flank pain and has no penicillin allergy. She asks whether treatment now means she will not need antibiotics in labour.
ask: What is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Observe without antibiotics because GBS urinary infection in pregnancy is not associated with neonatal risk.
Give intrapartum antibiotics only if a repeat vaginal swab at 36 weeks remains GBS positive.
Treat the current urinary infection and document an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
Give one oral penicillin dose now and avoid further treatment if urinary symptoms improve.
Plan elective caesarean delivery solely because GBS bacteriuria was detected during this pregnancy.
explanations: Symptomatic GBS bacteriuria warrants antenatal UTI treatment. It also identifies maternal colonisation and neonatal early-onset disease risk.

A repeat vaginal swab is not required after documented GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy. Intrapartum prophylaxis is indicated when labour or membrane rupture occurs, with elective prelabour caesarean an exception.

Correct: treat the symptomatic high-count GBS UTI with an appropriate antibiotic course and document GBS bacteriuria as an indication for intrapartum IV antibiotic prophylaxis, regardless of subsequent swab results.
One antibiotic dose is inadequate for a symptomatic UTI. Treatment should follow culture sensitivities and pregnancy-safe dosing guidance.
GBS colonisation alone is not an indication for caesarean birth. Prevention relies on appropriately timed intrapartum antibiotics when indicated.
pearl: GBS bacteriuria in the current pregnancy predicts colonisation and usually removes the need for a repeat screening swab.
pivot: Elective caesarean before labour with intact membranes does not require GBS-specific intrapartum prophylaxis, though surgical prophylaxis remains standard.

steps: Assess
Exclude pyelonephritis or sepsis and review urine culture susceptibility and pregnancy status.
Treat
Give a pregnancy-appropriate antibiotic course for symptomatic GBS UTI and assess response.
Flag labour
Document GBS bacteriuria clearly in antenatal records for intrapartum prophylaxis.
Coordinate
Counsel about labour presentation, rupture of membranes and neonatal risk assessment.
management.safety: Do not mistake antenatal UTI treatment for adequate intrapartum neonatal GBS prevention.
management.local: Queensland Clinical Guideline amended March 2025: GBS UTI warrants treatment at diagnosis and intrapartum prophylaxis.

skill: Epithelial ovarian cancer / germline risk assessment without family history
stem: A 54-year-old is newly diagnosed with high-grade serous epithelial ovarian carcinoma and is beginning multidisciplinary oncology care. She has no known relatives with breast or ovarian cancer and assumes genetic testing cannot help because her family history is negative.
ask: What is the best response?
options: Avoid genetic risk assessment because the absence of affected relatives excludes inherited cancer syndromes.
Screen only her adult daughters with CA-125 because germline testing cannot influence patient treatment.
Arrange immediate prophylactic oophorectomy for every female relative without establishing mutation status.
Offer genetic risk assessment and discuss germline testing through an appropriately supported pathway.
Delay all genetics discussion until five years after cancer treatment because results have no current value.
explanations: Many patients with pathogenic germline variants have no recognised family history. Lack of affected relatives does not exclude inherited predisposition.
CA-125 screening is not a reliable substitute for genetics assessment in asymptomatic relatives and does not identify a familial pathogenic variant.
Risk-reducing surgery in relatives requires individual genetic risk assessment and informed counselling; indiscriminate surgery causes avoidable harm.

Correct: all women newly diagnosed with invasive epithelial ovarian cancer should be offered genetic risk assessment. Germline testing may guide treatment options and enable cascade counselling and testing for relatives.
Genetic results can be relevant during current oncology treatment and family risk management, so a five-year delay is inappropriate.
pearl: High-grade serous ovarian cancer merits germline risk assessment even when family history appears negative.
pivot: A variant of uncertain significance should not automatically trigger irreversible preventive surgery in relatives.

steps: Counsel
Explain inherited susceptibility and why negative family history does not rule it out.
Refer
Arrange genetic risk assessment and consented germline testing through oncology/genetics services.
Integrate
Discuss results in the multidisciplinary team for treatment and surveillance implications.
Support family
Offer cascade counselling or testing to relatives if a pathogenic germline variant is found.
management.safety: Do not interpret absent family history or a variant of uncertain significance as definitive genetic risk information.
management.local: Cancer Australia: newly diagnosed invasive epithelial ovarian cancer warrants genetic risk assessment regardless of family history.

skill: Diabetic CKD with albuminuria / kidney-protective SGLT2 initiation
stem: A 61-year-old with type 2 diabetes has persistent albuminuria (urine ACR 48 mg/mmol), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m² and BP 128/76 mmHg on maximally tolerated losartan. HbA1c is 6.8% and she has no recurrent ketoacidosis, active foot ulcer or current volume depletion. She asks whether any further kidney-protective medication is useful despite reasonable glycaemia.
ask: Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Intensify insulin solely to lower HbA1c below 5% before considering renal-protective therapy.
Stop losartan because a reduced eGFR automatically contraindicates renin–angiotensin system blockade.
Start routine NSAID therapy because suppression of renal inflammation slows diabetic CKD progression.
Delay additional therapy until eGFR falls below 15 because current kidney function is too preserved.
Consider an SGLT2 inhibitor for renal protection with counselling, monitoring and sick-day precautions.
explanations: An HbA1c target below 5% is unsafe for many older patients and not the recommended route to kidney protection. SGLT2 benefits extend beyond glucose lowering.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce albuminuria and progression when tolerated; a stable eGFR of 32 is not itself a reason to stop losartan.
NSAIDs can precipitate AKI, especially in CKD or volume depletion, and are not kidney-protective disease-modifying therapy.
Waiting until kidney failure forfeits opportunities to slow progression. Evidence supports SGLT2 initiation at eGFR at least 20 in eligible diabetic CKD.

Correct: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce CKD progression and cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria at this eGFR, even when HbA1c is near target. Review contraindications and counsel about euglycaemic DKA and sick-day withholding.
pearl: Renal and cardiovascular benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetic CKD are not dependent on a markedly elevated HbA1c.
pivot: Acute illness, dehydration, fasting and planned surgery require temporary SGLT2 withholding to reduce ketoacidosis risk.

steps: Verify
Confirm persistent albuminuria, stable eGFR, potassium, BP and current medication tolerance.
Initiate
Discuss an SGLT2 inhibitor for renal protection alongside ongoing ARB and risk-factor care.
Counsel
Explain genital infection risk, hydration, sick-day rules and symptoms of ketoacidosis.
Review
Monitor renal function, volume status, adverse effects and albuminuria over follow-up.
management.safety: Do not continue SGLT2 inhibitors through significant fasting or acute illness without a sick-day plan.
management.local: RACGP type 2 diabetes recommendations updated November 2024: SGLT2 therapy reduces CKD progression at eGFR ≥20 with albuminuria.

skill: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome / preventing recurrent pregnancy loss
stem: A 31-year-old at 7 weeks' gestation has had three consecutive unexplained first-trimester miscarriages. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on two tests 13 weeks apart; anticardiolipin IgG is persistently high. She has never had a venous or arterial thrombosis, has normal platelets and no bleeding. An early scan confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy.
ask: Which intervention is most likely to improve the chance of live birth?
options: Commence low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin with specialist antenatal review.
Prescribe therapeutic-dose warfarin throughout pregnancy because antibodies confer a high thrombotic risk.
Use aspirin alone until the fetal anatomy scan excludes congenital abnormalities and growth restriction.
Defer all antithrombotic treatment until a placental Doppler abnormality confirms developing insufficiency.
Arrange prophylactic platelet transfusions every month to prevent antibody-mediated placental thrombosis.
explanations: Correct: recurrent pregnancy loss with persistently positive antiphospholipid tests supports obstetric APS. Low-dose aspirin combined with prophylactic LMWH from early pregnancy improves outcomes; coordinate dosing and postpartum thrombosis prevention with obstetric and haematology teams.

Warfarin crosses the placenta and risks fetal harm; therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation is generally reserved for APS with a thrombotic history or other specific indications, not isolated obstetric APS.
Aspirin alone does not provide the same evidence-supported live-birth benefit as aspirin plus heparin in established obstetric APS. The indication exists now rather than after the anomaly scan.
Waiting for abnormal Dopplers misses the opportunity for early placental protection. APS-related pregnancy loss can occur before detectable fetal growth restriction or Doppler changes.
Platelet transfusion treats selected severe thrombocytopenic bleeding, not antiphospholipid antibody-mediated pregnancy loss. Routine transfusions add risks without preventing placental thrombosis.
pearl: Distinguish obstetric APS without thrombosis from thrombotic APS: anticoagulant intensity and postpartum plans differ.
pivot: If antiphospholipid antibodies are absent and loss is unexplained, routine aspirin/heparin has not shown live-birth benefit.

steps: Confirm phenotype
Review pregnancy-loss history, repeat antibody timing, thrombosis history and current pregnancy viability.
Prevent recurrence
Coordinate low-dose aspirin and prophylactic LMWH promptly with maternal-fetal medicine and haematology.
Surveil pregnancy
Monitor fetal growth, blood pressure, pre-eclampsia risk, bleeding and anticoagulant tolerance.
Plan delivery
Arrange neuraxial-anaesthesia anticoagulant timing and individualised postpartum prophylaxis and follow-up.
management.safety: Do not substitute warfarin for LMWH in early pregnancy or use therapeutic-dose heparin reflexively without thrombotic indications.
management.local: Australasian recurrent pregnancy loss clinical management guideline, 2024; individualise aspirin and LMWH dosing locally.

skill: Adolescent PCOS / avoid ultrasound overdiagnosis
stem: A 16-year-old, three years after menarche, reports persistent cycles 60–90 days apart, progressive hirsutism and troublesome acne. Pregnancy is excluded, and thyroid function, prolactin and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. An ultrasound requested elsewhere shows multiple small follicles, and she worries this alone proves severe ovarian disease.
ask: What is the most appropriate diagnostic approach at this stage?
options: Diagnose PCOS solely from ovarian follicle number because adolescent cycles are usually irregular.
Assess ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism without using ultrasound morphology as a diagnostic criterion.
Use anti-Müllerian hormone instead of clinical features because it is more reliable before adulthood.
Reassure that menstrual irregularity at any point after menarche cannot indicate endocrine pathology.
Start infertility medication immediately before confirming a diagnosis or discussing her current goals.
explanations: Polycystic-appearing ovaries are common during normal adolescent maturation and are not diagnostic. The sonographic appearance should not displace careful assessment of symptoms and alternative endocrine causes.

Correct: adolescent PCOS diagnosis requires both persistent ovulatory dysfunction and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism after exclusion of mimics. Ultrasound and AMH are not recommended for diagnosis within eight years of menarche.
AMH may substitute for ultrasound in some adults, but it should not be used to diagnose adolescent PCOS. Its cut-offs and physiological variation can promote false-positive labels.

Some cycle irregularity is physiological early after menarche, but sustained oligomenorrhoea at three years with hirsutism warrants evaluation. Dismissing the presentation misses metabolic and psychological needs.

Ovulation induction is for appropriately assessed infertility, not a first response to a teenager seeking diagnostic clarity and symptom relief. Management should reflect her preferences and contraception needs.
pearl: For adolescents, require both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism; neither ovarian ultrasound nor AMH establishes PCOS.
pivot: If only one feature is present, label 'at increased risk' and arrange reassessment rather than prematurely diagnosing PCOS.

steps: Clarify features
Document cycle intervals, hyperandrogenism, pubertal timing, medications and pregnancy possibility.
Exclude mimics
Assess thyroid, prolactin, non-classic CAH and other causes when clinically indicated.
Support symptoms
Discuss acne/hirsutism options, cycle protection, lifestyle and mental health without weight stigma.
Follow longitudinally
Screen metabolic risks and revisit diagnostic criteria as reproductive maturity progresses.
management.safety: Do not interpret multifollicular ovaries or a single elevated AMH as proof of adolescent PCOS.
management.local: Monash-led 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline, adolescent diagnostic criteria.

skill: Palpable breast lump / discordant triple assessment
stem: A 46-year-old notices a new firm, irregular 2-cm breast lump. Diagnostic mammography and targeted ultrasound are reported as probably benign, but the palpable lesion remains clinically suspicious and a small ipsilateral axillary node is palpable. She asks whether reassuring imaging means biopsy can safely be omitted.
ask: What is the safest next step in investigating this discordance?
options: Repeat routine population screening in two years because diagnostic imaging is already reassuring.
Prescribe empirical antibiotics and repeat imaging only if the lump becomes tender or red.
Arrange breast specialist assessment and image-guided or clinically directed core biopsy despite benign imaging.
Reassure that the axillary node is reactive and discharge after one normal mammogram report.
Request serum tumour markers first because normal values would exclude an invasive breast malignancy.
explanations: Population screening is designed for asymptomatic people; a suspicious palpable mass requires diagnostic assessment now. A long interval could delay detection of a mammographically occult tumour.
Antibiotics are not justified without convincing infective features such as erythema, warmth or fever. A hard irregular mass and node are not typical uncomplicated mastitis.

Correct: clinical examination, imaging and tissue sampling form the triple assessment. A suspicious or discordant component warrants specialist review and tissue diagnosis; benign imaging cannot overrule persistent concerning clinical findings.

Axillary lymphadenopathy alongside a suspicious mass raises rather than resolves concern. Even technically adequate imaging can miss malignancy, particularly with dense tissue or certain tumour types.
Serum tumour markers have inadequate sensitivity and specificity to rule out early breast cancer. They do not replace histopathology when examination remains suspicious.
pearl: The triple assessment is concordance-based; a suspicious clinical examination still needs resolution despite reassuring imaging.
pivot: A soft, mobile lump with concordant benign examination and imaging may follow a different safety-net pathway.

steps: Examine
Document mass site, size, mobility, skin and nipple changes plus axillary and supraclavicular nodes.
Reconcile tests
Review the quality and lesion concordance of targeted ultrasound and diagnostic mammography.
Obtain tissue
Refer promptly for specialist-directed core biopsy of the palpable abnormality and suspicious node.
Close loop
Track pathology, arrange multidisciplinary review if malignant and communicate results with clear follow-up.
management.safety: Do not substitute screening intervals, tumour markers or empirical antibiotics for biopsy of a persistently suspicious mass.
management.local: Cancer Australia triple-test guidance for investigation of new breast symptoms.

skill: Primary adrenal insufficiency / confirm and localise
stem: A 35-year-old reports months of fatigue, postural dizziness, salt craving and weight loss. Examination shows diffuse hyperpigmentation, BP 94/58 mmHg without shock, and laboratory tests show sodium 128 mmol/L and potassium 5.5 mmol/L. At 8 am, cortisol is low and ACTH markedly elevated; she is alert and tolerating oral intake.
ask: Which investigation best confirms the suspected endocrine diagnosis when clinically stable?
options: Perform an oral glucose tolerance test to exclude diabetes as the cause of her weight loss.
Obtain a pituitary MRI before testing because the ACTH result suggests central adrenal failure.
Measure a random afternoon cortisol repeatedly and treat only if every result remains low.
Arrange a short ACTH stimulation test using laboratory-specific cortisol response thresholds.
Order urinary catecholamines as the definitive investigation for adrenal cortex insufficiency.
explanations: Diabetes can cause weight loss, but hyperpigmentation, hyperkalaemia and high ACTH strongly point to primary adrenal failure. Glucose testing would not establish cortisol reserve.
High ACTH suggests loss of adrenal negative feedback, not primary pituitary ACTH deficiency. Pituitary MRI is reserved for suspected central disease or relevant neurological features.
Random cortisol is influenced by circadian rhythm and illness and is not a robust confirmatory strategy. A morning sample and dynamic testing are more interpretable.

Correct: the short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test evaluates adrenal cortisol reserve in a stable patient. Elevated baseline ACTH with inadequate stimulated cortisol supports primary adrenal insufficiency; interpret against the local assay.
Urinary catecholamines investigate selected catecholamine-secreting tumours, not adrenal cortical failure. They cannot explain the cortisol–ACTH pattern or confirm Addison disease.
pearl: Low morning cortisol plus high ACTH points to primary adrenal insufficiency; Synacthen response confirms inadequate reserve.
pivot: If hypotension, vomiting or altered consciousness develops, treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately without waiting for stimulation testing.

steps: Assess stability
Check haemodynamics, glucose, sodium, potassium and features of impending adrenal crisis.
Confirm
Arrange morning cortisol/ACTH review and short Synacthen test with assay-specific cut-offs.
Treat cause
Start supervised glucocorticoid replacement and mineralocorticoid when indicated; investigate autoimmunity.
Prevent crisis
Provide sick-day rules, emergency hydrocortisone plan, medical alert and endocrine follow-up.
management.safety: Never delay emergency parenteral hydrocortisone for confirmatory testing in a patient with suspected adrenal crisis.
management.local: RCPA Manual short Synacthen test, reviewed February 2026; confirm assay-specific cut-offs.

skill: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia / intracranial haemorrhage prevention
stem: A well-looking term neonate develops widespread petechiae within hours of birth. Platelets are 9 × 10⁹/L, haemoglobin and coagulation studies are normal, and the mother has a normal platelet count. A previous sibling had unexplained severe neonatal thrombocytopenia. Cranial ultrasound has been requested but is not yet available.
ask: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment and investigation strategy?
options: Observe without treatment because the baby is clinically well and clotting studies are normal.
Give vitamin K alone and repeat the platelet count after routine discharge the next day.
Administer oral prednisolone to the mother to raise the newborn platelet count rapidly.
Delay platelet treatment until cranial imaging demonstrates an intracranial haemorrhage.
Urgently involve neonatology and transfusion medicine for compatible platelets and IV immunoglobulin.
explanations: Severe thrombocytopenia in an apparently well neonate can still cause catastrophic intracranial bleeding. A count below 10 × 10⁹/L requires urgent specialist treatment, not outpatient observation.
Vitamin K prevents vitamin-K-deficiency bleeding but does not correct alloimmune platelet destruction. Normal coagulation tests and profound isolated thrombocytopenia indicate a different mechanism.
Maternal oral steroids cannot rapidly treat the newborn's dangerously low platelet count. The baby needs immediate neonatal haemostatic support and diagnostic evaluation.
Waiting for intracranial bleeding defeats prevention; ultrasound is important but must not postpone indicated platelet support. Haemorrhage may be clinically silent early.

Correct: suspect fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia with severe isolated thrombocytopenia, normal maternal platelets and affected sibling. Urgently arrange appropriate platelet transfusion, IVIg when indicated, cranial imaging and maternal/paternal platelet-antigen studies.
pearl: Severe isolated neonatal thrombocytopenia with normal maternal platelets suggests alloimmune destruction and silent intracranial bleeding risk.
pivot: If the mother also has immune thrombocytopenia, neonatal thrombocytopenia may be autoimmune rather than alloimmune; management still depends on severity.

steps: Stabilise
Assess bleeding, neurological status and platelet count; minimise traumatic procedures.
Protect haemostasis
Urgently obtain compatible platelet support and consider IVIg under neonatal/transfusion protocols.
Investigate
Perform cranial ultrasound and HPA antibody/typing studies with transfusion specialists.
Plan recurrence
Arrange maternal-fetal medicine counselling because future pregnancies can be affected more severely.
management.safety: Do not defer platelet support for neuroimaging in a neonate with profound thrombocytopenia.
management.local: Australian National Blood Authority Ig Governance criteria for neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.

skill: Borderline personality disorder / structured psychological treatment
stem: A 24-year-old with longstanding affective instability, impulsive self-injury, fear of abandonment and unstable relationships has no current psychosis or mania. After assessment, she denies imminent suicidal intent and collaborates on a safety plan. She asks for a treatment that builds skills to manage repeated interpersonal crises and self-harm urges.
ask: Which ongoing therapeutic approach most directly addresses these difficulties?
options: Offer structured dialectical behaviour therapy alongside collaborative risk assessment and continuity of care.
Prescribe long-term high-dose benzodiazepines as the main intervention for emotional regulation and impulsivity.
Recommend repeated brief admissions whenever interpersonal conflict arises, without outpatient skills training.
Use antipsychotic polypharmacy indefinitely because personality disorder symptoms imply underlying psychosis.
Advise avoidance of close relationships until distressing thoughts and emotions have completely disappeared.
explanations: Correct: DBT combines acceptance and change strategies, including distress tolerance, emotion regulation, mindfulness and interpersonal effectiveness. It is an evidence-supported structured therapy for recurrent self-harm and emotion dysregulation, integrated with ongoing safety assessment.
Benzodiazepines do not teach coping skills and can worsen disinhibition, dependence and overdose risk. Medication may target specific comorbid conditions but is not a substitute for psychotherapy.

Hospital admission can be necessary for acute safety, but automatic repeated admissions without a community treatment plan may undermine autonomy and continuity. Match crisis response to current risk.
BPD does not itself imply psychosis, and routine antipsychotic polypharmacy lacks a sound long-term rationale. Reassess for comorbid illness before considering targeted medication.

Avoidance of relationships reinforces isolation and does not build interpersonal effectiveness. DBT explicitly teaches safer communication, boundary setting and distress management within valued relationships.
pearl: DBT develops skills in four areas: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness.
pivot: Active suicidal intent, inability to maintain immediate safety or severe intoxication requires urgent crisis assessment before routine psychotherapy.

steps: Assess risk
Review suicidal intent, means, recent self-injury, protective factors and coexisting disorders at each relevant contact.
Plan therapy
Offer structured DBT or another evidence-based personality-disorder psychotherapy with shared goals.
Coordinate care
Agree on a crisis plan, consistent follow-up, family involvement when appropriate and treatment of comorbidities.
Review function
Track self-harm frequency, emotional regulation, relationships, service use and quality of life.
management.safety: A diagnosis of BPD must never be used to dismiss genuine acute suicide risk or physical injury.
management.local: Australian healthdirect DBT clinical overview and structured psychological care principles.

skill: Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage / urgent cardiac repair
stem: A newborn develops marked cyanosis and tachypnoea soon after delivery. SpO₂ remains 75% despite oxygen; chest radiography shows diffuse pulmonary oedema with a relatively small heart. Echocardiography identifies pulmonary veins draining below the diaphragm with severe obstruction and an interatrial communication. The infant is becoming acidotic.
ask: Which management priority best addresses the underlying cause of deterioration?
options: Give repeated inhaled bronchodilators because pulmonary oedema in newborns usually reflects bronchospasm.
Urgently stabilise in intensive care and arrange cardiac surgical correction of obstructed venous return.
Start routine diuretics and schedule elective repair after several weeks of feeding and weight gain.
Close the interatrial communication immediately because atrial mixing is the source of hypoxaemia.
Administer prostaglandin alone and wait for ductal patency to resolve the pulmonary venous obstruction.
explanations: Bronchodilators do not relieve obstruction to pulmonary venous drainage. The cyanosis, oedema and echocardiographic anatomy indicate a mechanical cardiovascular emergency.

Correct: obstructed TAPVD causes pulmonary venous hypertension, oedema and severe hypoxaemia. Provide neonatal intensive-care respiratory and circulatory support and urgent paediatric cardiac surgery to reconnect pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
Diuretics may be adjunctive in selected settings but cannot relieve fixed pulmonary venous obstruction. Delaying repair risks progressive acidosis, pulmonary injury and circulatory collapse.
An interatrial communication allows oxygenated pulmonary venous blood reaching the right atrium to access systemic circulation. Closing it before definitive repair could eliminate essential mixing.
Prostaglandin is lifesaving in selected duct-dependent lesions, but obstructed TAPVD is not corrected by opening the ductus. Do not let empiric ductal therapy delay expert diagnosis and surgery.
pearl: Severe neonatal cyanosis with pulmonary oedema and obstructed anomalous pulmonary veins is a surgical emergency.
pivot: Unobstructed TAPVD may present later with pulmonary overcirculation and a less dramatic oxygenation deficit.

steps: Stabilise
Call neonatal intensive care, support oxygenation and ventilation, correct acidosis and assess perfusion.
Define anatomy
Obtain urgent expert echocardiography and identify the site of pulmonary venous obstruction.
Definitive action
Arrange immediate transfer and paediatric cardiac surgical repair without elective delay.
Follow through
Monitor postoperative pulmonary vein patency, pulmonary pressures and feeding/growth.
management.safety: Do not assume oxygen-refractory cyanosis is primary lung disease or that prostaglandin relieves pulmonary venous obstruction.
management.local: Children's Health Queensland TAPVD clinical information developed by Queensland Paediatric Cardiac Service.

skill: Pertussis vaccination / closely spaced pregnancies
stem: A 28-year-old attends antenatal care at 25 weeks, eight months after her previous delivery. She received a pertussis-containing vaccine in the previous pregnancy and a tetanus booster four years ago. She has no vaccine contraindications and asks whether the short interval makes another pertussis dose unnecessary.
ask: Which recommendation best protects her newborn against pertussis?
options: Defer vaccination until after birth because maternal antibody transfer is insufficient before delivery.
Repeat vaccination only if serum pertussis antibody testing shows that her titre is below range.
Give a pertussis-containing vaccine now because a dose is recommended during every pregnancy.
Wait until 36 weeks because earlier vaccination increases the risk of neonatal infection.
Omit antenatal vaccination if all adult household contacts have already received pertussis boosters.
explanations: Postpartum vaccination cannot provide the same transplacental antibody protection during early infancy. Antenatal immunisation reduces severe infant pertussis risk.
Pertussis antibody titres are not routinely used to determine maternal vaccine eligibility. There is no validated titre threshold that replaces the recommendation for each pregnancy.

Correct: a single dTpa dose is recommended in every pregnancy, ideally at 20–32 weeks, even when pregnancies are closely spaced. Antibodies cross the placenta and protect infants before their own vaccine series.
Vaccination at 36 weeks is possible if missed earlier, but 20–32 weeks optimises antibody production and transfer. Deliberate delay may leave an infant born early less protected.
Cocooning household contacts helps reduce exposure but cannot replace direct transplacental maternal antibodies. Maternal vaccination remains recommended irrespective of household vaccine status.
pearl: Maternal dTpa is recommended in every pregnancy, ideally at 20–32 weeks, irrespective of a recent prior dose.
pivot: If the recommended window has passed, vaccinate as soon as practical up to delivery rather than withholding the dose.

steps: Check history
Confirm gestation, prior doses, severe allergy history and other pregnancy vaccine needs.
Vaccinate
Offer dTpa during this pregnancy now; use locally funded recommended formulation.
Counsel
Explain passive infant protection, common injection-site effects and why repeat pregnancy doses matter.
Document
Record vaccination, discuss influenza and RSV vaccination as indicated, and plan infant immunisation.
management.safety: Do not rely on a previous pregnancy's dTpa dose or household cocooning alone for newborn protection.
management.local: Australian Immunisation Handbook pertussis vaccination in pregnancy, updated October 2026.

skill: Sulfonylurea poisoning / recurrent hypoglycaemia and octreotide
stem: A 3-year-old is found drowsy beside an opened container of a grandparent's gliclazide. Bedside glucose is 1.9 mmol/L and consciousness improves after IV dextrose, but hypoglycaemia recurs twice despite a glucose infusion. The child has stable vital signs and no evidence of other ingestion.
ask: What additional therapy most directly prevents further recurrent hypoglycaemia?
options: Increase repeated dextrose boluses indefinitely without suppressing endogenous pancreatic insulin secretion.
Give activated charcoal several hours later as the only treatment for recurrent neuroglycopenia.
Start a glucagon infusion alone because it reliably blocks sulfonylurea-stimulated insulin release.
Administer octreotide with monitored glucose support and toxicology-guided observation in hospital.
Discharge once awake because initial neurological improvement excludes delayed sulfonylurea effects.
explanations: Dextrose rescues hypoglycaemia but can stimulate further insulin release in sulfonylurea poisoning. Repeated boluses without an insulin-suppressing strategy promote rebound episodes.
Activated charcoal may have a limited early role after selected ingestions, but it does not treat established recurrent hypoglycaemia. Toxicology advice is needed for decontamination decisions.
Glucagon may transiently increase glucose but does not suppress beta-cell insulin secretion and can worsen rebound hypoglycaemia. It is not the preferred antidote.

Correct: octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin release and reduces recurrent hypoglycaemia after sulfonylurea exposure. Continue IV dextrose as needed, check bedside glucose frequently and observe after stopping treatment.
Sulfonylureas can cause prolonged or delayed hypoglycaemia after apparent recovery, particularly in children. Discharge after a single normal glucose reading is unsafe.
pearl: Sulfonylurea toxicity causes insulin-driven recurrent hypoglycaemia; octreotide prevents the rebound that dextrose alone may perpetuate.
pivot: A child exposed only to metformin has a different toxicity profile; sulfonylurea-specific octreotide is not routine.

steps: Resuscitate
Treat symptomatic hypoglycaemia immediately with IV glucose and monitor airway and consciousness.
Block insulin
Start octreotide under paediatric toxicology guidance while titrating dextrose support.
Investigate
Check serial bedside glucose, electrolytes and possible co-ingestants; involve a poisons service.
Observe
Continue inpatient monitoring after stopping dextrose and octreotide for delayed recurrence before discharge.
management.safety: One sulfonylurea tablet can cause life-threatening delayed hypoglycaemia in a toddler; do not discharge early.
management.local: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne oral hypoglycaemic poisoning guideline; use age-appropriate local octreotide dosing.

skill: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea / test of cure and partner management
stem: A 22-year-old has asymptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhoea detected by NAAT after an oral-sex exposure. She received the recommended Australian ceftriaxone-based regimen, and symptoms were absent throughout. She asks whether a negative urine NAAT in three months is sufficient follow-up for the throat infection.
ask: What follow-up strategy is most appropriate for the pharyngeal infection?
options: Avoid any follow-up because pharyngeal infection cannot persist after an intramuscular antibiotic.
Repeat only a urine NAAT at three months because throat sampling is technically unreliable.
Perform an immediate throat NAAT tomorrow because residual bacterial nucleic acid disappears overnight.
Give a second empirical antibiotic course now before assessing microbiological treatment response.
Arrange site-specific pharyngeal test of cure and later reinfection testing with partner management.
explanations: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea has greater potential for treatment failure and antimicrobial resistance. Clinical improvement or lack of symptoms does not establish eradication.
A urine sample does not assess the pharyngeal site and may miss persistent throat infection. Three-month retesting addresses reinfection but not early microbiological cure.
Testing immediately after treatment may detect nonviable gonococcal DNA and yield misleading NAAT positivity. Follow local timing guidance, commonly at least two weeks for NAAT.

Routine repeat antibiotics without evidence of failure increases antimicrobial pressure and adverse effects. Culture and susceptibility testing are important when persistence or resistance is suspected.

Correct: arrange throat-specific test of cure using locally recommended culture/NAAT timing, plus reinfection testing around three months and contact tracing. WA guidance recommends NAAT no earlier than two weeks after treatment.
pearl: Test of cure must sample the originally infected anatomical site; NAAT too soon may detect residual nonviable organisms.
pivot: If a follow-up throat test is positive, seek culture and susceptibility advice to distinguish persistent infection from reinfection.

steps: Confirm treatment
Review the actual antibiotic regimen, culture availability, allergies and antimicrobial susceptibility information.
Test throat
Arrange pharyngeal test of cure at the locally recommended interval; avoid premature NAAT.
Protect contacts
Offer partner notification, other STI screening and abstinence advice until treatment conditions are met.
Prevent reinfection
Arrange repeat STI testing around three months and consider HIV PrEP eligibility where appropriate.
management.safety: A negative urine test cannot exclude persistent pharyngeal gonorrhoea; follow current jurisdictional TOC guidance.
management.local: WA Health gonorrhoea guidance and Australian STI Guidelines; local site-specific TOC policies may vary.
